8.content:
The **battle of the Great Plains** was fought in 203 BC in modern [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia") between a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") army commanded by [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus"), and allied [Carthaginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") and [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") armies commanded by [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Gisco "Hasdrubal Gisco") and [Syphax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syphax "Syphax") respectively. The battle was part of the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") and resulted in a heavy defeat for Carthage.

In the wake of its defeat in the [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") (264–241 BC) Carthage expanded its territory in south-east [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal). When the Second Punic War broke out in 218 BC a Roman army landed in north-east Iberia. After a [disastrous Roman setback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Upper_Baetis "Battle of the Upper Baetis") in 211 BC, Scipio took command in 210 BC and cleared the peninsula of Carthaginians in five years. He returned to Rome determined to carry the war to the Carthaginian homeland in North Africa. Appointed [consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consul "Consul") in 205 BC Scipio spent a year in [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") training his army and accumulating supplies. [In 204 BC the Romans landed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_/(204%E2%80%93201_BC/) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") with four [legions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion "Roman legion") near the Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia") and [besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege") it. The Carthaginians and their Numidian allies each set up their own camps about 11 kilometres (7 mi) from the Romans but close to each other. After several months of little activity Scipio launched a [surprise night attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Utica_/(203_BC/) "Battle of Utica (203 BC)") on both camps, overrunning them and setting fire to much of both. Carthaginian and Numidian casualties were heavy.

The Carthaginians reformed their army in an area known as the Great Plains, 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica. They were reinforced by 4,000 Iberian warriors to a total of about 30,000 men. Hearing of this, Scipio immediately marched most of his army to the scene. The size of his army is not known, but it was outnumbered by the Carthaginians. After several days of skirmishing, both armies committed to a [pitched battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle"). Upon being charged by the Romans all of those Carthaginians who had been involved in the debacle at Utica turned and fled; morale had not recovered. Only the Iberians stood and fought. They were enveloped by the well-drilled Roman legions and wiped out.

Syphax and his Numidians were pursued, brought to battle at [Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirta "Cirta"), and [again defeated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"); Syphax was captured. The Roman ally [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa") took over his kingdom. Scipio moved his main army to [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), within sight of the city of Carthage. Scipio and Carthage entered into peace negotiations, and Carthage recalled armies from Italy commanded by [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal") and [Mago Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca"). The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it. The following year the Carthaginians raised another army, incorporating Hannibal and Mago's recalled veterans. This was also defeated by Scipio, at the [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama"). Carthage [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace") and accepted a humiliating [treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty "Treaty"), ending the war.

The [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") was fought between the two main powers of the western [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") in the 3rd century BC: [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-3) The war lasted for 23 years, from 264 to 241 BC, and was fought primarily on the Mediterranean island of [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily"), its surrounding waters and in [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa").[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-3) The Carthaginians were defeated[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996157-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199997-5) and by the terms of the [Treaty of Lutatius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lutatius "Treaty of Lutatius") evacuated Sicily and paid Rome an [indemnity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indemnity "Indemnity") of 3,200 silver [talents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talent_/(measurement/) "Talent (measurement)")[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-8) over ten years.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011196-9) Four years later, Rome seized [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia") and [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") on a cynical pretence and imposed a further 1,200 talent indemnity,[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-10)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006569-11)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011209,_212%E2%80%93213-12) actions which fuelled Carthaginian resentment.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015211-13)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011213-14) The near-contemporary [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece") historian [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") considered this act of bad faith by the Romans to be the single greatest cause of war with Carthage breaking out again nineteen years later.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996175-15)

From 236 BC [Carthage expanded its territory in Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_Iberia "Carthaginian Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal).[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011220-16) In 226 BC the [Ebro Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_Treaty "Ebro Treaty") with Rome established the [Ebro River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_River "Ebro River") as the northern boundary of the Carthaginian [sphere of influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_of_influence "Sphere of influence").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006143%E2%80%93144-17) A little later Rome made a separate treaty of association with the city of [Saguntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saguntum "Saguntum"), well south of the Ebro.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144-18) In 219 BC [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"), the de facto ruler of Carthaginian Iberia, led an army to Saguntum and [besieged, captured and sacked it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Saguntum "Siege of Saguntum").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-19)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144%E2%80%93145-20) In early 219 BC Rome [declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_war "Declaration of war") on Carthage, starting the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006145-21)

[![Image 1: a map of the western Mediterranean region showing the territory controlled by Rome and Carthage in 218 BC](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg/500px-Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg)

The approximate extent of territory controlled by Rome and Carthage immediately before the start of the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War")

In 218 BC Hannibal led a large Carthaginian army from Iberia through [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Gaul#During_the_Republic "Roman Gaul"), [over the Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") and invaded [mainland Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Italy "Mainland Italy"). During the next three years Hannibal inflicted heavy defeats on the Romans at the battles of [the Trebia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trebia "Battle of the Trebia"), [Lake Trasimene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Trasimene "Battle of Lake Trasimene") and [Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae "Battle of Cannae").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-22) At the last of these alone, at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999192%E2%80%93194-23) The historian Toni Ñaco del Hoyo describes these as "great military calamities",[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-22) Brian Carey writes that they brought Rome to the brink of collapse.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey20072-24) Hannibal's army campaigned in Italy for a further 14 years before the survivors withdrew.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015322-25)

There was also extensive fighting in [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians"), Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa. In 211 BC the Romans suffered a severe reverse at the [battle of the Upper Baetis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Upper_Baetis "Battle of the Upper Baetis") and were penned back by the Carthaginians to the north-east corner of Iberia. In 210 BC Roman reinforcements stabilised the situation;[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015322-25) later that year [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus")[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-27) arrived with further Roman reinforcements to take command in Iberia.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-28) In a carefully planned assault in 209 BC [he captured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cartagena_/(209_BC/) "Battle of Cartagena (209 BC)") the centre of Carthaginian power in Iberia, [New Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Spain "Cartagena, Spain").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-28)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015292-29) During the following four years Scipio repeatedly defeated the Carthaginians and drove them out of Iberia in 205 BC.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006277%E2%80%93285-30)

[![Image 2: a photograph of an inverted, polished, slightly tarnished, battered bronze hemisphere](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg/250px-Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg)

The bowl of a [Montefortino-type helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montefortino_helmet "Montefortino helmet"), which was used by Roman infantry between c. 300 BC and 100 AD. The cheek guards are missing.

Most male Roman citizens were liable for military service and would serve as [infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infantry "Infantry"), a [better-off minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equites "Equites") providing a [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") component. Traditionally, when at war the Romans would raise two [legions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion "Roman legion"), each of 4,200 infantry – this could be increased to 5,000 in some circumstances,[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199923-31) or, rarely, even more.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-32) – and 300 cavalry. Approximately 1,200 of the infantry – poorer or younger men unable to afford the armour and equipment of a standard [legionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legionary "Legionary") – served as [javelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin "Javelin")\-armed [skirmishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skirmisher "Skirmisher") known as [velites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velites "Velites"); they each carried several javelins, which would be thrown from a distance, a short sword and a 90-centimetre (3 ft) shield.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200648-33) The balance were equipped as [heavy infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_infantry "Heavy infantry"), with [body armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_armor "Body armor"), a large [shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutum_/(shield/) "Scutum (shield)") and [short thrusting swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladius "Gladius"). They were divided into three ranks, of which the front rank, known as _[hastati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastati "Hastati")_, also carried two javelins; the second and third ranks, known as _[principes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principes "Principes")_ and _[triari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triari "Triari")_ respectively, had a [thrusting spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasta_/(spear/) "Hasta (spear)") instead. Both legionary [sub-units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maniple_/(military_unit/) "Maniple (military unit)") and individual legionaries fought in relatively open order.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200653-34)

It was the long-standing Roman procedure to elect two men each year as senior [magistrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_magistrate "Roman magistrate"), known as [consuls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul"), who in time of war would each lead an army. An army was usually formed by combining a Roman legion with a similarly sized and equipped legion provided by their [Latin allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socii "Socii"); allied legions usually had a larger attached complement of cavalry than Roman ones.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922%E2%80%9325-35)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-36) By this stage of the war, Roman armies were generally larger, typically consisting of four legions, two Roman and two provided by its allies, for a total of approximately 20,000 men. The Roman army which invaded Africa consisted of four legions, each of the Roman pair reinforced to an unprecedented 6,200 infantry and with a more usual 300 cavalry each. Modern historians estimate the army to have totalled 25,000–30,000 men, including perhaps 2,500 cavalry.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650,_227,_287-37)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-38)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011309-39)

Carthaginian citizens only served in their army if there was a direct threat to the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage").[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby19989-40)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006494-41) When they did they fought as well-armoured heavy infantry armed with long thrusting spears, although they were notoriously ill-trained and ill-disciplined. In most circumstances Carthage recruited foreigners to make up its army.[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-43) Many were from North Africa and these were frequently referred to as "[Libyans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Libya "Ancient Libya")". The region provided several types of fighters, including: [close order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_order_formation "Close order formation") infantry equipped with large shields, helmets, short swords and long thrusting [spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear "Spear"); javelin-armed [light infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_infantry "Light infantry") skirmishers; close order shock cavalry[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-45) (also known as "heavy cavalry") carrying spears; and light cavalry skirmishers who threw javelins from a distance and avoided close combat. (The latter were usually [Numidians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians").)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-46)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201579%E2%80%9387-47) The close order African infantry and the citizen-militia both fought in a tightly packed formation known as a [phalanx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phalanx "Phalanx").[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-48) On occasion some of the infantry would wear captured Roman armour.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015305-49) As well both Iberia and Gaul provided experienced but unarmoured infantry who would charge ferociously, but had a reputation for breaking off if a combat was protracted. [Slingers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sling_/(weapon/) "Sling (weapon)") were frequently recruited from the [Balearic Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_Islands "Balearic Islands").[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-46)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19998%E2%80%939-50)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings199690-51)

[Pitched battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle") were usually preceded by the two armies camping 2–12 kilometres (1–7 mi) apart for days or weeks; sometimes forming up in battle order each day. If either commander felt at a disadvantage, they might march off without engaging. In such circumstances it was difficult to force a battle if either of the commanders was unwilling to fight.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200656-52)[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199664-53) Forming up in battle order was a complicated and premeditated affair, which took several hours. Infantry were usually positioned in the centre of the battle line, with light infantry skirmishers to their front and cavalry on each flank.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200657-54)

In 206 BC Scipio left Iberia and returned to Italy.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285-55) He was denied the [triumph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") he would normally have expected on the grounds that he had not occupied any of the magistracies of the _[cursus honorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cursus_honorum "Cursus honorum")_, the sequential mixture of military and political administrative positions held by aspiring Roman politicians.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999268-56) Aged 31 he was elected to the senior position of consul in early 205 BC, despite not meeting the minimum age for the position of 42.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200799-57) Scipio was already anticipating an invasion of North Africa and while still in Spain had been negotiating with the Numidian leaders [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa") and [Syphax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syphax "Syphax"). He failed to win over the latter, but made an ally of the former.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285%E2%80%93286-58)

Opinion was divided in Roman political circles as to whether an invasion of North Africa was excessively risky. Hannibal was still on Italian soil; there was the possibility of further Carthaginian invasions,[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-59) shortly to be realised when [Mago Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca") landed in [Liguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liguria "Liguria");[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-60) the practical difficulties of an amphibious invasion and its logistical follow up were considerable; and when the Romans had invaded North Africa in 256 BC during the First Punic War they had been driven out with heavy losses, which had re-energised the Carthaginians.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286%E2%80%93287-61) Eventually a compromise was agreed: Scipio was given Sicily as his consular province,[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194-62) which was the best location for the Romans to launch an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland from and then logistically support it, and permission to cross to Africa on his own judgement.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-59) But Roman commitment was less than wholehearted: Scipio was not allowed to [conscript troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") for his consular army, as was usual, but could only call for volunteers.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998195-63)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-60)

In 216 BC the survivors of the Roman defeat at Cannae had been formed into two legions and sent to Sicily.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006218-64) They still formed the main part of the garrison of Sicily and Scipio used the many men who volunteered to increase the strength of each of these to an unprecedented 6,500.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-32) The total number of men available to Scipio and how many of them travelled to Africa is unclear; the Roman historian [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy "Livy"), writing 200 years later, gives totals for the invasion force of either 12,200, 17,600 or 35,000. Modern historians estimate a combat strength of 25,000–30,000, of whom more than 90 per cent were infantry.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-32)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-38) With up to half of the complement of his legions being fresh volunteers, and with no fighting having taken place on Sicily for the past five years, Scipio instigated a rigorous training regime. This extended from drill by individual [centuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centuria "Centuria") – the basic Roman army manoeuvre unit of 80 men – to exercises by the full army. This lasted for approximately a year. At the same time Scipio assembled a vast quantity of food and [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel"), [merchant ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_ship "Merchant ship") to transport it and his troops, and warships to escort the transports.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287%E2%80%93288-65)

Also during 205 BC 30 Roman ships under Scipio's second-in-command, the [legate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legatus "Legatus") [Gaius Laelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Laelius "Gaius Laelius"), raided North Africa around [Hippo Regius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippo_Regius "Hippo Regius"), gathering large quantities of loot and many captives.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006288-66)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-38) The Carthaginians initially believed this was the anticipated invasion by Scipio and his full invasion force; they hastily strengthened fortifications and raised troops – including some units made up of Carthaginian citizens. Reinforcements were sent to Mago in an attempt to distract the Romans in Italy.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194%E2%80%93195-67) Meanwhile a succession war had broken out in Numidia between the Roman-supporting Masinissa and the Carthaginian-inclined Syphax. Laelius re-established contact with Masinissa during his raid. Masinissa expressed dismay regarding how long it was taking the Romans to complete their preparations and land in Africa.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998198%E2%80%93199-68)

[![Image 3: A relief map of part of north Africa, showing the site of the battle and the movements of Scipio's forces during the campaign](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png/500px-Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa,_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png)

In 204 BC, probably in June or July, the Roman army left Sicily in 400 transport ships, escorted by 40 [galleys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley "Galley").[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-69) Three days later[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-70) they disembarked at [Cape Farina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Farina "Cape Farina") 20 kilometres (12 mi) north of the large Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia").[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-69) The locals fled and Carthage's immediate response, a scouting party of 500 cavalry, was defeated with the loss of its commander and the general in overall charge of responding to the invasion. The area was pillaged and 8,000 captives were sent back to Sicily as slaves or hostages. Masinissa joined the Romans with either 200 or 2,000 men, the sources differ. A large fortified camp was established on a rocky peninsula near [Ghar el-Melh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghar_el-Melh "Ghar el-Melh")[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999275-71)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200663-72) which was known as _Castra Cornelia_. Masinissa had been recently defeated by his Numidian rival Syphax, wounded and had his army scattered. Syphax had been persuaded to take firm action in support of Carthage by the Carthaginian general [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Gisco "Hasdrubal Gisco") and by his assertive new wife: Hasdrubal's daughter [Sophonisba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophonisba "Sophonisba").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006290%E2%80%93292-73)

Carthage sent a larger party to probe the Roman position, about 4,000 soldiers under a general called Hanno. His command of mixed Numidians and Carthaginian citizens based itself at Salaeca, 24 kilometres (15 mi) from the Romans, and did little scouting. Following a [stratagem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruse_de_guerre "Ruse de guerre") agreed with Scipio, Masinissa's cavalry raided Hanno's force who chased them off and then pursued them into a Roman ambush. Hanno died in a sharp conflict during which 1,000 of his men were killed or taken prisoner. The survivors were in turn pursued for 50 kilometres (30 mi), only 1,000 escaped. The Romans pillaged an ever-wider area, sending their loot and prisoners to Sicily in the ships bringing their supplies.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292-74)

Wanting a more permanent base and a port more resilient to the bad weather to be expected when winter came, Scipio [besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besiege "Besiege") Utica. Despite the Romans being well supplied with [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine") the siege dragged on[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-70)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998206-75) and a Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal set up a fortified camp 11 kilometres (7 mi) from the Romans with a reported 33,000 men. Syphax joined him, establishing his own camp 3 kilometres (2 mi) away from Hasdrubal's with a reported 60,000 troops. The size of both of these armies as reported by ancient historians has been questioned by their modern counterparts as being infeasibly large. Nevertheless, it is accepted that the Romans were considerably outnumbered, in particular in terms of cavalry.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-76)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996207-77) The modern historian Dexter Hoyos suggests a combined Numidian and Carthaginian total of 47,500 men.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b203-78) The Romans pulled back from Utica to _Castra Cornelia_, where they were themselves now blockaded on the landward side.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294-79) Being outnumbered, Scipio was reluctant to commit his army to a pitched battle. Hasdrubal in turn was aware that two years earlier an army led by him in Iberia had been heavily defeated by a much smaller Roman army commanded by Scipio at the [battle of Ilipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ilipa "Battle of Ilipa") and so was himself reluctant to commit to a battle.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-80) He knew that more troops were being recruited in Iberia and was happy to pause hostilities until they joined his army.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b204-81)

Scipio sent [emissaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador") to Syphax to attempt to persuade him to defect. Syphax in turn offered to broker peace terms.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-76) A series of exchanges of negotiating parties followed, the sessions lasting several days.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278-82) With his delegations Scipio sent junior officers disguised as slaves to report back on the layout and construction of the Numidian camp, as well as the size and composition of the Numidian army and the most frequented routes in and out of the camp.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-76)[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-80) The Carthaginian camp was solidly constructed, with earthen ramparts and timber-built [barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks "Barracks"), but the Numidian one less so, with no clearly defined perimeter and the accommodation for the soldiers being largely constructed of [reeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed_/(plant/) "Reed (plant)") and roofed with [thatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thatch "Thatch").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-80)

As the weather improved Scipio made conspicuous preparations to assault Utica.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278%E2%80%93279-83) Instead, he marched his army out late one evening and divided it in two.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293-84)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-85) One part [launched a night attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Utica_/(203_BC/) "Battle of Utica (203 BC)") on the Numidian camp, setting fire to their reed barracks. In the ensuing panic and confusion the Numidians were dispersed with heavy casualties.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007105%E2%80%93106-86) Not realising what was happening, many Carthaginians set off in the dark to help extinguish what they assumed was an accidental blaze in their allies' camp. Scipio attacked them with the remaining Romans, stormed their camp and set fire to many of the Carthaginians' wooden huts. Again the Romans inflicted heavy casualties in the dark.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293%E2%80%93294-87)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007105%E2%80%93106-86)

Hasdrubal fled 40 kilometres (25 mi) to Carthage with 2,500 survivors, pursued by Scipio. Syphax escaped with a few cavalry and regrouped 11 kilometres (7 mi) away.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-85)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-88) With no Carthaginian field army to threaten them, the Romans pressed their siege of Utica and pillaged an extensive area of North Africa with strong and far-ranging raids. As well as gold and slaves the Romans accumulated large amounts of foodstuffs. This was added to the extensive stocks already built up by shipping grain from Sicily.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)

When word of the defeat reached Carthage there was panic, and some senators wanted to renew the peace negotiations. The Carthaginian Senate also heard demands for Hannibal's army to be recalled. A decision was reached to fight on with locally available resources.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294-79)[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-85) A force of 4,000 Iberian warriors finally arrived in Carthage, although their strength was exaggerated to 10,000 to maintain morale. Hasdrubal raised further local troops with whom to reinforce the survivors of Utica.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-90) Syphax remained loyal and joined Hasdrubal with what was left of his army.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294%E2%80%93295-91) The combined force is estimated at 30,000 and they established a strong camp on a flat plain of the [Bagradas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagradas_River "Bagradas River") known as the Great Plains. This was near modern Souk el Kremis[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89) and about 120 kilometres (75 mi) from Utica.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200663-72) Hasdrubal assembled this substantial force within 30–50 days of the defeat at Utica.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-90)

[![Image 4: A black and white sketch of a cavalryman from the ancient era carrying two spears and a shield](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/Sacred_Band_cavalryman.png/250px-Sacred_Band_cavalryman.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sacred_Band_cavalryman.png)

Carthaginian cavalryman, as depicted in 1891

When he heard that the Carthaginians were reassembling their army, Scipio left a force to continue the siege of Utica and led the rest on a rapid march to the Great Plains. His army did not take a [baggage train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Train_/(military/) "Train (military)"), which suggests that Scipio was intent on bringing the Carthaginians to battle as soon as possible. It is not known how large this army was, but it was smaller than the Carthaginian; the modern historian Brian Carey suggests that it was about 20,000 strong.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-88) The Romans established a fortified camp approximately 6 kilometres (4 mi) from that of the Carthaginians. For three days there were skirmishes between the lighter troops of both sides, but their main forces stayed in camp. On the fourth day, nine days after Scipio had left Utica, both commanders formed up their full armies and they advanced towards each other.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)

Both armies deployed in the usual formation. Hasdrubal placed his newly arrived Iberian infantry in the centre of his line, with the Carthaginian infantry who had survived the battle at Utica on their right, and to their right his Carthaginian cavalry. To the left of the Iberians were Syphax's Numidian infantry and to their left Numidian cavalry.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89) The two Roman legions took position in the centre of their line, deployed in their customary three lines. An allied legion deployed in similar fashion on each side of the Romans.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-88) On the Roman right flank were the cavalry attached to the four legions with Laelius in command; the Numidian cavalry under Masinissa were on the left flank.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106%E2%80%93107-92)

The two armies approached each other and the battle opened when the cavalry on each flank charged. Then either both units of Carthaginian cavalry broke on contact and were routed, or possibly turned and fled without attempting to counter-charge their attackers. The two legions of Latin allies charged the opponents facing them and again the Carthaginian and Numidian infantry put up little or no resistance before turning and fleeing.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015333-93)[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89) It is possible that these troops started to flee as soon as their flanking cavalry did, well before the Latin allies contacted them.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007108-94) Many of the men of these units had been involved in the recent debacle of the burning camps at Utica and the memory of having been beaten by the same Roman army reduced their morale to the point that they had no stomach for the fight. The Roman cavalry and the two Latin legions pursued their opponents off the battlefield.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-89)

The Iberians however charged home against the _hastati_ in the front rank of the two Roman legions and fought fiercely. Once he saw that his _hastati_ were holding their own Scipio did not follow normal practice, which would have been to feed in men from the second rank of _principes_ to replace casualties and relieve tired fighters. Instead he had the _principes_ and _triari_ of each legion form a column, march parallel to the line of battle and then round to attack the Iberians in the [flank and rear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanking_maneuver "Flanking maneuver").[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295%E2%80%93296-95) Thus enveloped, the Iberians fought to the death and were wiped out. A large proportion of the rest of the Carthaginian army succeeded in escaping.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings199690-51)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295%E2%80%93296-95) Most of these [deserted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desertion "Desertion") rather than rallying to either Hasdrubal or Syphax.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999281-96)

The historian [Nigel Bagnall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Bagnall "Nigel Bagnall") considers it a "foolish decision" by Hasdrubal to fight a battle with an army consisting entirely of men who were either demoralised or new recruits and whose state of training was "deplorably low". He describes the Roman army as "battle-hardened" and as having high morale. He suggests that Scipio's rapid march from Utica forced the Carthaginians into a battle before they were ready.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999280%E2%80%93281-97)

[![Image 5: An ancient battle scene in metal relief](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Scenes_from_the_Battle_of_Zama_MET_149866.jpg/250px-Scenes_from_the_Battle_of_Zama_MET_149866.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scenes_from_the_Battle_of_Zama_MET_149866.jpg)

Hasdrubal fled to Carthage, where he was demoted and exiled.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-98) Syphax and his Numidians were pursued, brought to battle outside his capital, [Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirta "Cirta"), and [again defeated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"), Syphax being captured.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-98) Cirta surrendered to Masinissa, who took over Syphax's kingdom.[\[note 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-100)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998212-99) Scipio moved his main army to [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), within sight of the city of Carthage.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282,_284-101) Scipio and Carthage entered into peace negotiations, while Carthage recalled both Hannibal and Mago from Italy.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-102) The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999287%E2%80%93291-103)

Hannibal was placed in command of another army, formed of his and Mago's veterans from Italy and newly raised troops from Africa, with 80 [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant") but few cavalry.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-104) The decisive [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") followed in October 202 BC.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-105) After a prolonged fight the Carthaginian army collapsed; Hannibal was one of the few to escape the field.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-105)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007118-106)

The peace treaty the Romans subsequently imposed on the Carthaginians stripped them of all their overseas territories and some of their African ones. An indemnity of 10,000 silver talents[\[note 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-107) was to be paid over 50 years. Hostages were taken. Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants and its fleet was restricted to 10 warships. It was prohibited from waging war outside Africa, and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BC. Henceforth it was clear Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007132-108) Scipio was awarded a triumph and received the _[agnomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus".[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011318-109)

3.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_ref-27)** Publius Scipio was the bereaved son of the previous Roman co-commander in Iberia, also named [Publius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Cornelius_Scipio_/(consul_218_BC/) "Publius Cornelius Scipio (consul 218 BC)"), and the nephew of the other co-commander, [Gnaeus Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnaeus_Cornelius_Scipio_Calvus "Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011268,_298%E2%80%93299-26)
4.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Great_Plains#cite_ref-43)** Roman and Greek sources refer to these foreign fighters derogatively as "mercenaries", but the modern historian Adrian Goldsworthy describes this as "a gross oversimplification". They served under several arrangements: some were the regular troops of allied cities or kingdoms seconded to Carthage as part of formal treaties; some were from allied states fighting under their own leaders; many were volunteers from areas under Carthaginian control who were not Carthaginian citizens. The Second Punic War: The Year 203 BCE
======================================

[Messalla](https://corvinus.nl/author/messalla/ "View all posts by Messalla") [06/06/2017](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/) 27/12/2018[Roman history](https://corvinus.nl/category/roman-history/), [The Mid-Republic (264-133 BCE)](https://corvinus.nl/category/roman-history/the-mid-republic-264-133-bce/), [The Second Punic War: Scipio (210-201 BCE)](https://corvinus.nl/category/roman-history/the-second-punic-war-scipio-210-201-bce/)

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Scipio-Africanus.jpg?resize=262%2C300&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/Scipio-Africanus.jpg?ssl=1)Scipio Africanus.

**[![Image 9](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/Vlag-NL.png?resize=51%2C34&ssl=1)](https://corvinus.nl/2018/12/03/de-annalist-het-jaar-203-bce/)Summary**

*   Publius Cornelius Scipio annihilates the armies of Hasdrubal and Syphax in a night attack near Utica;
*   Scipio again defeats Hasdrubal and Syphax at the Battle of Great Plains;
*   The Carthaginians finally decide to recall Hannibal from Southern Italy;
*   Gaius Laelius and Masinissa defeat King Syphax and capture him;
*   Masinissa captures Cirta and wants to marry Sophonisba, King Syphax’ Carthaginian wife; this is prevented by Scipio;
*   The Romans and Carthaginians agree to a truce; a delegation is sent to Rome to talk about peace and Hannibal lands in Africa near Hadrumetum;
*   The praetor Publius Quinctilius Varus and the proconsul Marcus Cornelius Cethegus defeat Mago Barcas in the territory of the Insubres. Mago is severely wounded and dies while sailing back to Africa;
*   The war in Africa continues after the Carthaginian capture dozens of Roman cargo ships.

The new consuls Gnaeus Servilius Caepio and Gaius Servilius Geminus were granted Bruttium and Etruria as their respective provinces. Although their family names may suggest otherwise, they were at best distant relatives. Caepio was from a patrician branch of the _gens Servilia_, while Geminus was a plebeian. However, the latter’s grandfather was probably Publius Servilius Geminus, the patrician consul of [252 BCE](https://corvinus.nl/2016/05/24/the-annalist-the-years-254-251-bce/) and [248 BCE](https://corvinus.nl/2016/05/24/the-annalist-the-years-248-243-bce/). The consul of [217 BCE](https://corvinus.nl/2017/05/13/the-annalist-the-year-217-bce/), Gnaeus Servilius Geminus, possibly an uncle or cousin of Gaius, was also a patrician, so obviously the Servilii Gemini were originally all patricians.

[![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Forum-Romanum2.jpg?resize=400%2C300&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/04/Forum-Romanum2.jpg?ssl=1)View of the Forum Romanum.

Either Gaius Servilius Geminus himself or his father (also named Gaius) had gone over to the plebs, a procedure known as the _transitio ad plebem_. By being adopted by a plebeian, a patrician lost his original status. While we have a very [famous case](https://corvinus.nl/2017/03/27/publius-clodius-pulcher-an-aristocratic-peoples-tribune-and-bad-boy/) from the Late Republic of a patrician going over to the common people, we do not know what Gaius’ or his father’s motives were.[\[1\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn1) Gaius senior had been a member of a Roman senatorial committee sent north to oversee the distribution of land in the new Latin colonies of Placentia and Cremona. He had been captured by the Boii in [218 BCE](https://corvinus.nl/2017/05/13/the-annalist-the-year-218-bce/) and was long presumed dead. When it turned out that he was alive after all, this had legal consequences for his son, as we will see below.

But first we must turn to Africa. Although the Romans still had 20 legions in the field and 160 warships in service, all that really counted were the parts of the army and fleet serving in Africa. That is where the war would be decided. Scipio’s proconsular command had been prolonged again, this time until the war had been ended. The proconsul was still threatening Utica and he hoped to bring King Syphax, who perhaps by now had grown tired of his Carthaginian wife, back on the Roman side. Scipio devised a plan that was both legally questionable and morally indefensible. But it worked perfectly, and apparently the end justified the means.

_A night attack near Utica_

[![Image 11](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Stater1.jpg?resize=400%2C194)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Stater1.jpg)Stater from Carthage, third century BCE (source: [Classical Numismatic Group Inc.](https://www.cngcoins.com/)).

During the **winter**, there had been some negotiations between the Romans and their enemies. Scipio’s envoys had discovered that the Carthaginians had built timber barracks in their camp, while the Numidians slept in huts made of thatched reeds and straw mats. So in other words, both camps had a lot of combustible material. During the negotiations, Syphax had constantly proposed that the Carthaginians leave Italy and the Romans Africa, and that for the territories in between the status quo would be leading (i.e. they would belong to the party that controlled them). Scipio pretended to be interested, but instead of sending camp servants (_calones_) with his envoys, he picked some senior centurions[\[2\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn2) and dressed them up as slaves. This gave them an excellent opportunity to thoroughly look around in the enemy camp and gauge the strength of the enemy troops.

At the beginning of **spring**, Scipio pretended to be preparing for an attack on Utica. He had siege equipment installed aboard his warships, as if he was planning to assault the city from the sea. He also had 2.000 men occupy a hill overlooking Utica. At the same time, he had sent envoys to the Numidian camp again who had asked Syphax whether the Carthaginians would accept the peace terms proposed by the king as well. As it turned out, Hasdrubal, son of Gisgo, was prepared to sign a peace treaty. But when Scipio was informed of this news, he immediately ordered his envoys to go back and tell the enemy that the deal was off. He feigned to be personally in favour of the peace terms, but claimed that they had been rejected by his _consilium_, the war council comprising the tribunes, legates and most senior centurions of the legions (_primipili_). This was a lie of course, but Scipio needed a pretext to attack the enemy camps. Livius claims that the Carthaginians and Numidians had added some unfavourable terms to the draft treaty, but that sounds like a later invention to justify Scipio’s bad faith. Polybius does not mention such terms at all. On the contrary, he considered the action that was to follow Scipio’s “most splendid and most adventurous”.[\[3\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn3)

[![Image 12](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/North-Africa-202.jpg?resize=940%2C521)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/North-Africa-202.jpg)Map of North Africa (source: [Ancient World Mapping Center. “À-la-carte”](http://awmc.unc.edu/awmc/applications/alacarte/); CC BY 4.0).

The proconsul decided to stage a daring night attack on both enemy camps. He set out from his camp at the end of the _prima vigilia_ (first watch), possibly around 21:00. The distance to the enemy camps was about 11 kilometres, and Scipio’s army reached them around midnight. Half of the army and all the Numidians were given to Laelius and Masinissa with instructions to attack the Numidian camp. Scipio himself marched on Hasdrubal’s camp with the rest of the army. The Romans managed to take their adversaries completely by surprise. Laelius and Masinissa quickly stormed King Syphax’ camp. The soldiers threw their torches and soon the entire camp was on fire. Many Numidians, most of whom had been asleep when the attack commenced, perished in the flames or were trampled to death by their comrades. The survivors were cut down by Laelius’ and Masinissa’s men.

The Carthaginians had noticed the great fire from their own camp and at first did not suspect any foul play. They assumed the fire had started by accident and some of them rushed out of the gates to provide aid. This was the moment Scipio had been waiting for. He ordered his soldiers to attack and many of the men that had gone out to help were quickly surrounded and killed. Scipio’s soldiers then pursued the survivors into the enemy camp and set it ablaze as well, the flames quickly consuming the timber barracks. Tens of thousands of men died in both attacks, but Syphax and Hasdrubal managed to get away. Scipio’s action had been highly dubious, but there could be no doubt that it had been brilliantly executed and that his night attack was a complete success.

_The Battle of Great Plains_

After Hasdrubal’s army had been all but wiped out, the _shophtim_ convened the Council of Thirty Elders to discuss the current situation. Some were in favour of sending envoys to Scipio to discuss peace terms, others wanted to recall Hannibal from Italy. But Hasdrubal and members of the pro-Barcid faction supported a third position, i.e. raising a new army and persuading King Syphax not to withdraw from the war. A majority of the Elders ultimately supported this position, and just at that moment, 4.000 Celtiberian mercenaries arrived from Spain.[\[4\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn4) Syphax began arming Numidian peasants, and soon the Carthaginians and their Numidian allies had an army of some 30.000 men in the field again. These numbers may look impressive, but only the Celtiberians seem to have had any battle experience.

[![Image 13](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/roman_infantry_hastati_INFO.jpg?resize=160%2C210)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/roman_infantry_hastati_INFO.jpg)Hastatus (source: Europa Barbarorum).

[![Image 14](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/roman_infantry_polybian_triarii_INFO.jpg?resize=160%2C210)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/roman_infantry_polybian_triarii_INFO.jpg)Triarius (source: Europa Barbarorum).

The next confrontation took place at the Great Plains (_Magni Campi_), a five days march southwest of Utica. On the fourth day after arriving on the plains, both commanders deployed their army in battle order and attacked. The Italian and Masinissa’s Numidian cavalry quickly routed the Carthaginian and Numidian horsemen on both flanks, leaving the infantry exposed. The Carthaginian infantry and Syphax’ Numidian foot soldiers do not seem to have put on much of a fight, leaving the 4.000 Celtiberians isolated in the centre to fight to the death. These men fought well and their resistance allowed much of the Carthaginian army to escape. Ultimately they were pinned down by the Roman _hastati_. Scipio then had his lines of _principes_ and _triarii_ wheel from line into column formation and march to the flanks. There they turned again, marched forward and began enveloping the Celtiberians. Most of these were killed and the Romans won another victory, but Hasdrubal and Syphax managed to get away.

_Carthaginian attack at Utica_

Scipio now divided up his army into two parts. Laelius and Masinissa were given ten maniples of infantry and most of the cavalry and ordered to march west and defeat King Syphax, who was clearly reeling after so many defeats. At the same time, Scipio and the rest of the army marched on various African cities, causing many of them to surrender and taking others by storm. Again there was a huge panic in Carthage and again the Elders deliberated on what to do. Many proposals were adopted, combining military and diplomatic actions. It was decided to send the fleet to Utica to attack the Romans there that still had the city under a loose siege. At the same time Hannibal was recalled from Southern Italy and Carthage’s own defences were strengthened. Diplomacy was also given a chance and a new delegation was set up to travel to Scipio for negotiations.

[![Image 15](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Ostia.jpg?resize=500%2C191)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Ostia.jpg)Mosaic from Ostia.

Meanwhile, Scipio had occupied Tunis, a city a mere 20 kilometres from Carthage, but also the site of a [serious Roman defeat](https://corvinus.nl/2016/05/24/the-annalist-the-years-256-255-bce/) during the First Punic War. Tunis could be seen very well from Carthage and vice versa, and suddenly the Romans spotted many warships leaving the Carthaginian harbour. Scipio immediately realised that Utica was their target and that his fleet was in serious danger. His ships had been converted into siege engines and were in no condition for a naval battle. The Roman commander hurried back to Utica, perhaps taking his cavalry ahead. He arrived just in time to prepare for the Carthaginian attack, but Scipio knew that he could only fight a defensive battle. He therefore had several transport ships lashed together so that they formed huge platforms from which his soldiers could fight off the Carthaginian attacks. Livius compared the ensuing battle to an attack by ships on solid walls. Although the Romans managed to save their valuable warships, the Carthaginians managed to cut free and tow away some 60 transport ships, constituting about 15% of the entire Roman transport fleet. Surely this was a setback for Scipio, but it could have been far worse.

_Syphax defeated and captured_

Laelius and Masinissa had marched west for some two weeks. They easily defeated the troops that were still occupying the territories of the Massylii, Masinissa’s tribe. After securing Masinissa’s throne, they advanced further and invaded the lands of the Masaesyli to confront King Syphax. Syphax had raised another army, but it was mostly made up of raw recruits. The Roman infantry and Numidian cavalry worked closely together and easily routed Syphax’ inexperienced army. When the king’s horse was wounded, it threw its rider and Syphax was taken prisoner and brought to Laelius. Masinissa was now given permission to advance on Cirta, the capital of the Masaesyli in present-day Algeria.

[![Image 16](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/MASSINISSA_-_MAA_23_-_87000716.jpg?resize=400%2C189)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/MASSINISSA_-_MAA_23_-_87000716.jpg)Coin with the image of Masinissa or his son Micipsa (source: [Classical Numismatic Group, Inc.](https://www.cngcoins.com/), CC BY-SA 2.5 license).

Masinissa easily captured Cirta and went to the royal palace. There he met Sophonisba, wife of King Syphax and daughter of Hasdrubal, son of Gisgo. She implored him to protect her against the Romans. Masinissa, perhaps genuinely in love with the woman, decided to marry her and ordered a ceremony to take place that same day. When Laelius arrived in Cirta, he quickly learned what had happened and was not amused. He tried to take Sophonisba away and send her to Scipio with the other prisoners, but Masinissa begged him to let her stay and let Scipio decide about her fate.

Laelius ultimately agreed, unwilling to risk losing a valuable ally over a woman. Only Syphax and some of the other prisoners were sent to the proconsul. When Scipio heard about Masinissa and Sophonisba, he was not amused either. He rebuked his ally and told him that King Syphax had been captured under Roman auspices. His wife therefore belonged to the Romans and Masinissa could not marry her. Masinissa had no option but to accept Scipio’s judgment. Fulfilling his promise to the woman that she would not fall into Roman hands, he brought her a cup of poison. Sophonisba took the cup without hesitation and committed suicide.

_Negotiations and Hannibal’s return_

[![Image 17](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/Mommsen_p265.jpg?resize=250%2C392)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/Mommsen_p265.jpg)Hannibal Barcas

Scipio sent Laelius to Rome with Syphax and some of the other important prisoners. Upon his arrival, the Romans celebrated four days of public thanksgiving. The former king was first imprisoned in Alba Fucens and later in Tibur (now the town of Tivoli). Livius claims that the Carthaginians sent a delegation of 30 senior senators (_triginta seniorum principes_) to Scipio to negotiate. The Carthaginians had a Council of Thirty Elders and a larger Council of 104, and Livius’ claim suggests that the Carthaginians now sent all their Elders to the Roman commander to discuss peace terms. Scipio knew that his position was strong and the terms that he offered were extremely harsh and humiliating. The Carthaginians decided to accept the terms for the moment, knowing that Hannibal’s return to Africa might still change the situation. A truce (_indutiae_) was agreed and the Carthaginians sent a delegation to Rome to talk about peace.

By then, another delegation had already reached Hannibal in Southern Italy. The Carthaginian commander had fought one final battle on Italian soil this year, fighting the consul Gnaeus Servilius Caepio to a draw near Croton, but even Livius admits that the details of the battle are not clear. Our historian also claims that Hannibal “gnashed his teeth, groaned, and almost shed tears when he heard what the delegates had to say”, i.e. that he was ordered to return to Africa. All his victories had been good for nothing, but he had no choice but to embark his core troops and sail back to Carthage, the city that the 45-year-old general had last seen when he was a boy of nine. Livius furthermore claims that before leaving Italy, Hannibal massacred many Italians that refused to follow him to Africa. It seems likely, however, that our historian was merely echoing anti-Carthaginian propaganda here.

In **autumn**, Hannibal landed near Hadrumetum (now the city of Sousse), south of Carthage. Livius claims that the troops that were with him were mostly Bruttians and our historian did not think highly of them. However, it seems much safer to accept that the majority of these men were the highly experienced Spanish and African troops that had fought with Hannibal in Italy for many years. Polybius certainly suggests they were his elite troops. Perhaps with the addition of these veterans the Carthaginians would still be able to turn the tide of the war in their favour.

_Mago’s defeat and death_

[![Image 18](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Celt.jpg?resize=250%2C485)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Celt.jpg)Some Celtic war gear.

It was, however, clear that Hannibal would have to fight the Romans without the aid of his brother Mago. Mago had been roaming free in Liguria for some two years, but this year he was confronted and defeated by two Roman armies led by the praetor Publius Quinctilius Varus[\[5\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn5) and the proconsul Marcus Cornelius Cethegus. The battle took place at an unknown location in the territory of the Insubres, a Celtic tribe. Livius’ account of the battle is confused, but it is clear that it was a bloody fight and by no means an easy Roman victory. 2.300 Romans were killed and 5.000 Carthaginians. Mago was severely wounded, but managed to escape to the Gulf of Genua, where he met with representatives from Carthage that summoned him back to Africa. Sailing back to Africa with the remains of his army, Hannibal’s younger brother died of his wounds near Sardinia.

The consul Gaius Servilius Geminus had not achieved anything on the battlefield, but he did manage to free his father, who had been held prisoner by the Boii for fifteen years (see above). Geminus had been plebeian aedile in [209 BCE](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-209-bce/).[\[6\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn6) His election to this office had been unsuccessfully challenged by his political opponents, who argued that it violated a very obscure law of an unknown date.[\[7\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn7) This law stipulated that it was forbidden for citizens to hold strictly plebeian offices (i.e. those of people’s tribune and plebeian aedile) if their father had held a curule office (i.e. an office open to members of both classes) and was still alive. The rationale of this law is not entirely clear, but there is no need to discuss it here in detail.[\[8\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftn8) Now that his father, who had held a curule office, turned out to be alive, it was established that Geminus had indeed violated the law, so a special bill had to be passed by the popular assembly to absolve him of his ‘crime’.

_The war continues_

**Late in the autumn**, the Carthaginian delegation sent to Italy for peace negotiations had reached Rome, but was not allowed to cross the sacred boundary of the city, the _pomerium_. The envoys were therefore lodged in the _Villa Publica_, the base of operations for the censors on the Field of Mars, and apparently also used as a sort of hotel for foreign guests. They subsequently met with the senators in the temple of Bellona, but according to Livius, the negotiations came to nothing and the former consul Marcus Valerius Laevinus even accused the envoys of being spies. However, Polybius repeatedly claims that the Senate and popular assembly ratified the peace treaty, so it is not entirely clear what really happened in Rome.

[![Image 19](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Bellona.jpg?resize=400%2C300)](https://i0.wp.com/corvinus.nl/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Bellona.jpg)Remains of the temple of Bellona (in the foreground).

In a fiercely competitive environment like that of Rome, many men were eager to take over Scipio’s command in Africa and steal his victory and glory. The consul Caepio, for instance, had left Italy for Sicily and was planning to cross the sea to Africa to join the fight there. He had to be recalled by Publius Sulpicius Galba, who had been nominated dictator specifically for this occasion. Galba then began touring Italy, now free from enemy troops, to investigate the position that various cities had taken during the war.

Even if a peace treaty had been accepted by the Romans, it was soon in tatters anyway when **late in the autumn** or **early in the next year** the Carthaginians captured dozens of Roman cargo ships loaded with provisions. These ships had sailed from Sicily to Africa, but had been driven off course and got stranded near Carthage. The crews had fled, and the jubilant Carthaginians had confiscated the ships and provisions. Scipio considered this a violation of the armistice and immediately sent a committee of three men to Carthage to protest. These men were molested by the furious Carthaginians and then ambushed when they sailed back to Utica on their quinquereme. The ship was lost, but the delegates managed to get away with their lives. It was now clear that the war would continue. It was also clear that the great statesman and general Quintus Fabius Maximus would not see the end of the war. He died this year, probably well into his seventies. His son, the consul of [213 BCE](https://corvinus.nl/2017/05/13/the-annalist-the-year-213-bce/), had died the year before.

**Sources**

_Primary sources_

*   Livius, Ab urbe condita, [Book 29.38](http://mcadams.posc.mu.edu/txt/ah/Livy/Livy29.html) and [Book 30.1-30.26](http://mcadams.posc.mu.edu/txt/ah/Livy/Livy30.html);
*   Polybius, The Histories, [Book 14.1-14.10](http://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/14*.html) and [Book 15.1-15.4](http://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Polybius/15*.html).

_Secondary sources_

*   Rachel Feig Vishnia, [The _transitio ad plebem_ of C. Servilius Geminus](http://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/zpe/downloads/1996/114pdf/114289.pdf);
*   Adrian Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage, p. 293-300;
*   Andrew Lintott, The Constitution of the Roman Republic, p. 117;
*   Richard Miles, Carthage must be destroyed, p. 310-312.

**Notes**

[\[1\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref1) For a discussion, see [this excellent article](http://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/zpe/downloads/1996/114pdf/114289.pdf) by Rachel Feig Vishnia.

[\[2\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref2) Livius uses the term _primi ordines_ (Liv. 30.4), but does so anachronistically. The _primi ordines_ were the (five) centurions of the first cohort of a legion. They were not known in the manipular legions of Scipio’s days.

[\[3\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref3) Polybius 14.5. The historian was heavily biased towards members of the _gens Cornelia_, such as Scipio. He tended to be blind to the latter’s sometimes questionable behaviour.

[\[4\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref4) “An interesting indication of the minimal control the Romans exercised over the greater part of the Spanish Peninsula” (Adrian Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage, p. 295).

[\[5\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref5) A distant ancestor of the Publius Quinctilius Varus who was defeated by Arminius in the Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE.

[\[6\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref6) He had also been curule aedile a year later.

[\[7\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref7) Livius 27.21.

[\[8\]](https://corvinus.nl/2017/06/06/the-annalist-the-year-203-bce/#_ftnref8) Once again, I refer to [this excellent article](http://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/zpe/downloads/1996/114pdf/114289.pdf) by Rachel Feig Vishnia.
