In 213 BC the struggle between Rome and Carthage in the Second Punic War reached a new intensity. By this point the war spanned the entire western and central Mediterranean. In Spain the rival Roman and Carthaginian forces had fought themselves to a stalemate. Despite remarkable successes, Hannibal made little headway against Rome in Italy in 214, and there too stalemate loomed. The protagonists now searched for new vulnerabilities in their enemy; Philip V of Macedon made alliance with Carthage and attacked the Roman position in Illyris (the First Macedonian War), while Rome encouraged King Syphax of the Masaesyles to move against Carthage in North Africa. Most importantly, in 213 the contest for Sicily reached a crescendo, with Roman forces commencing the siege of the city of Syracuse. Yet, inexplicably, in this crucial year, Hannibal seems uncharacteristically inactive and almost irrelevant. Hannibal’s summer campaign in 213 in the Salento is given only the briefest mention by Livy (25.1.1). Livy only reports that Hannibal “spent the summer in the territory of the Sallentini” and that “some insignificant cities of the Sallentini went over to him”. Clearly, Livy regarded it as being of little significance. Hannibal was the architect of Carthaginian grand strategy, Carthage’s most proven general, general of the war’s most successful, veteran army. Why then did Hannibal apparently accomplish so little in the summer of 213? Thanks to the extensive efforts of archaeology and field surveys (especially the Brindisino project of the Free University of Amsterdam) the economic and political changes in the Salento from the pre-Roman to post-Roman eras are perceptible, and able to be examined. Together with careful study of the ancient sources, I propose a more complete picture of the political, economic and demographic landscape of south-eastern Italy in 213. This, in turn, provides us with greater insight into Hannibal’s goals and accomplishments in his summer campaign that year.

[Ante bella punica: Western Mediterranean Military Development 350-264 BC](https://www.academia.edu/26292605/Ante_bella_punica_Western_Mediterranean_Military_Development_350_264_BC)

[Alastair Lumsden](https://st-andrews.academia.edu/AlastairLumsden)

This thesis investigates the military equipment and tactics utilized by Carthaginian, Celtic, Celtiberian, Iberian, Italic, Greek, Libyphoenican, Numidian, and Sicilian troops that fought in the Carthaginian, Roman, and Syracusan armies in the century leading up to the First Punic war. It also specifically examines the methods by which Carthage, Rome, and Syracuse extended their respective hegemonies and the socio-political power dynamics at work within them, which appear, like the aforementioned military equipment to have been remarkably similar. It intends to illustrate that this similar extension of hegemony and socio-political power dynamics worked together with their frequent employment of similar troops, who fought with similar weapons, to create a distinct western Mediterranean military koine. Therefore, this thesis refutes the traditional Roman-centric literary narratives that promoted a sense of Roman military exceptionalism during the fourth and early third centuries BC. Indeed, the corpus of archaeological evidence examined in this work demonstrates that Roman armies, which in the years following 338 consisted of up to fifty percent allies (many of whom had served in Carthaginian and Syracusan armies since the fifth century) were fighting with remarkably similar weapons and tactics as their wider western Mediterranean contemporaries. Finally, this thesis also intends to illustrate the central role that Celtic and central and southern Italians appear to have played in the development and transmission of this remarkably similar military equipment across the western Mediterranean.

32.content:
![Image 1: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_d07c07d4fa43459287b80100eb0f262e~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_123,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_d07c07d4fa43459287b80100eb0f262e~mv2.jpg)

**The Catapult (1868) by Edward Poynter (1836–1919)**, oil on canvas, Laing Art Gallery, Newcastle upon Tyne (Accession Number: TWCMS: B6377) This grand historical painting depicts Roman soldiers manning a siege engine during the Siege of Carthage (149–146 BCE). The dramatic scene showcases the intense preparation for an assault on the walls of Carthage, a pivotal moment in the Third Punic War, which ended in the city's total destruction. The imposing catapult, with its intricate wooden structure, dominates the composition, emphasizing the scale of Roman military engineering. Notably, the famous phrase attributed to Cato the Elder, "Delenda est Carthago" ("Carthage must be destroyed"), is carved into the wood of the catapult, referencing the persistent call for Carthage's annihilation, as recorded in [Plutarch's "Life of Cato" 27.1](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Plutarch/Lives/Cato_Major*.html#27). Image public domain courtesy of [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Catapulta_by_Edward_Poynter.jpg).

**The Roman Republic**

It could be argued that the Roman Republic reached its peak in the second half of the 2nd century BCE. The final war with Carthage, The Third Punic War (149-146 BCE), resulted in the complete destruction of this rival city. Rome was also expanding into Greece and the Hellenistic East, becoming the dominant power in the Mediterranean.

Wealth, slaves, and natural resources flowed into Rome from newly conquered provinces. The Senate's power was at its height, and traditional Republican ideals of shared governance and civic duty remained relatively intact, although cracks were beginning to show. Roman culture absorbed significant elements from Greek philosophy, art, and literature and there was in influx of Greek scholars, tutors, and artisans who elevated Roman intellectual life.

Roman law expanded with the growing scope of Roman control over provinces, and the legal foundations were formed that would influence future European legal systems.

Here are two older coins of Carthage.

![Image 2: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_098108a8dd8844d388c39bd94a2e3942~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_74,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_098108a8dd8844d388c39bd94a2e3942~mv2.jpg)

**Carthage**, First Punic War, Circa 264-241 BC, BI Dishekel, Carthage mint

**Obv:** Wreathed head of Tanit left; linear border

**Rev:** Horse standing right; palm tree in background

![Image 3: Carthage, Second Punic War. Circa 220-215 BC. Trishekel (Bronze, 29 mm, 20.32 g, 12 h). Head of Tanit to left, wearing wreath of grain ears, pendant earring and simple necklace. Rev. Horse standing right before palm tree. MAA 84. SNG Copenhagen 344. ](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_53cdacd7efb14e9c956a72de1219a246~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_73,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_53cdacd7efb14e9c956a72de1219a246~mv2.jpg)

Carthage, Second Punic War. Circa 220-215 BC. Trishekel (Bronze, 29 mm, 20.32 g, 12 h). Head of Tanit to left, wearing wreath of grain ears, pendant earring and simple necklace. Rev. Horse standing right before palm tree. MAA 84. SNG Copenhagen 344.

**The 3rd Punic War**

After the Second Punic War (218-201 BCE), Carthage was subjected to harsh terms under the Treaty of 201 BCE following the **Battle of Zama** in 202 BCE.

*   **Territorial Concessions**: Carthage was required to cede all territories outside of Africa to Rome.
    
*   **Restrictions on Warfare**: Carthage could not wage war, even within Africa, without Rome's explicit consent.
    
*   **Naval Limitations**: The Carthaginian navy was limited to ten ships, effectively neutralizing its maritime power.
    
*   **Financial Indemnity**: Carthage agreed to pay a substantial indemnity of 10,000 talents to Rome over a 50-year period.
    
*   **Hostages**: Carthage was to provide 100 hostages as a guarantee of compliance with the treaty terms.
    

Masinissa, was an ally of Rome during the Second Punic War, and became King of Numidia, a neighboring kingdom to the west of Carthage, and was granted Roman support as a client king. Masinissa took advantage of Carthage's inability to defend itself and began seizing Carthaginian territory, especially fertile agricultural land. His kingdom steadily grew at Carthage's expense. Rome was unsympathetic to Carthage's appeals for arbitration.

![Image 4: Kings of Numidia, Masinissa (203-148 BC) or his son, Micipsa (148-118 BC), Æ 26mm Obv: Laureate and bearded head to left Rev: Horse galloping to left; pellet below Ref: MAA 18a; Mazzard 50; SNG Copenhagen 505](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_11298417fb4548829bbc04c09b44e13e~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_75,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_11298417fb4548829bbc04c09b44e13e~mv2.jpg)

**Kings of Numidia, Masinissa** (203-148 BC) or his son, **Micipsa** (148-118 BC), Æ 26mm **Obv:** Laureate and bearded head to left **Rev:** Horse galloping to left; pellet below **Ref:** MAA 18a; Mazzard 50; SNG Copenhagen 505

When the Carthaginians struck out against Masinissa, they gave Rome suffifient reason to declare war. The Carthaginians tried to appease Rome and avoid a conflict. Carthage was already weakened by the losses against Masinissa and was in no position to battle Rome.

"They sent ambassadors to Rome to complain of Masinissa, and at the same time to accuse their own citizens of taking up arms against him too hastily and rashly, and of furnishing an occasion for an imputation of hostility on the part of their city. When one of the [senators](https://www.livius.org/articles/concept/senate/) asked the ambassadors why they did not condemn their officers at the beginning of the war instead of waiting till they were beaten, and why they did not send their embassy before, instead of postponing it till now, they could not give any answer."
-Appian, The Punic Wars, 15.74 

The city of Utica - 15 km from Carthage with a good port, gave themselves up to the Romans. With a strategic point from which to launch a war, the Roman Senate declared war.

The Senate, which had been previously eager and prepared for war, having gained the accession of a city so strong and so conveniently placed, now disclosed its purpose. Assembling in the Capitol (where they were accustomed to deliberate on the subject of war), the senators voted to declare war against Carthage.
-Appian, The Punic Wars, 15.75

**Carthage Destroyed**

The outcome of this 3rd Punic War is the end of Carthage. Scipio who gave the final orders to raze the city is described by Polybius in Book 39 Chapter 5:

At the sight of the city utterly perishing amidst the flames Scipio burst into tears, and stood long reflecting on the inevitable change which awaits cities, nations, and dynasties, one and all, as it does every one of us men. This, he thought, had befallen Ilium, once a powerful city, and the once mighty empires of the Assyrians, Medes, Persians, and that of Macedonia lately so splendid. And unintentionally or purposely he quoted,—the words perhaps escaping him unconsciously,—“"The day shall be when holy Troy shall fall.  And Priam, lord of spears, and Priam's folk."
-Polibius, [Histories, 39.5](http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0234%3Abook%3D39%3Achapter%3D5)

Scipio reflects on the potential for Rome too to one day suffer a similar end.

**A Denarius from 149 BC**

All of the above serves as a long introduction to this coin from the Roman republic - a coin from the year in which the 3rd Punic War started.

Beyond his role as a moneyer, there is nothing known about Gaius Junius, son of Gaius's life or political career. The Junia gens was a prominent plebeian family in Rome, who claimed to descend from the legendary founder of the Roman Republic, Lucius Junius Brutus. Family members include Marcus Junius Brutus, one of Julius Caesar's assassins. However, no direct evidence links Gaius Junius C. f. to these individuals.

![Image 5: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_b223497593984b809c8d5fda9adc4182~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_76,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_b223497593984b809c8d5fda9adc4182~mv2.jpg)

**Roman Republic, C. Iunius C.f.**, AR Denarius (19mm, 3.78g), Rome, 149 BC.

**Obv:** Helmeted head of Roma right, behind, X

**Rev:** The Dioscuri galloping r.; below horses, C·IVNI·C·F and ROMA in partial tablet

**Ref:** Crawford 210/1

Here is another denarius from the Roman Republic, issued in 57 BC that is worth mentioning. : Q. Marcius Rex, whose statue appears on the reverse of this coin, built the Aqua Marcia, the longest of Roman aqueducts of Rome, in circa 144-140 BC. It was paid for by the spoils of Carthage and Corinth, which were both destroyed in 146.

![Image 6: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_0710ea344704466185ef435966501059~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_84,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_0710ea344704466185ef435966501059~mv2.jpg)

**L. Marcius Philippus**, 57 BC. AR Denarius (20mm), Rome mint.

**Obv:** ANCVS Diademed head of Ancus Marcius to right; behind, lituus.

**Rev:** PHILIPIVS / A-Q-V-A (MAR) Aqueduct, on which is a statue of Q. Marcius Rex on a horse rearing to right with a plant below.

**Ref:** Crawford 425/1. RBW 1524. Sydenham 919.

There was an interest in colonizing a new city in North Africa during the time of Gaius Gracchus (123 BCE). The Senate put a stop to this project. It was not until about 102 years after the destruction of Carthage that is was reestablished as a Roman colony. Dio credits Julius Caesar:

"But in the case of Corinth and Carthage, those ancient, brilliant, and distinguished cities which had been laid in ruins, he \[Julius Caesar\] not only colonized them, in that he regarded them as colonies of the Romans, but also restored them in memory of their former inhabitants, in that he honoured them with their ancient names; for he bore no grudge, on account of the hostility of those peoples, towards places that had never harmed the Romans."
-Cassius Dio, [Roman History, Book XLIII.50.3](http://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/e/roman/texts/cassius_dio/43*.html#50.3) 

Appian explains that it was Julius Caesar's dream, and it was Augustus who made it reality.

At a still later time it is said that Cæsar, who afterwards became dictator for life, when he had pursued Pompey to Egypt, and Pompey's friends from thence into Africa, and was encamped near the site of Carthage, was troubled by a dream in which he saw a whole army weeping, and that he immediately made a memorandum in writing that Carthage should be colonized. Returning to Rome not long after, and while making a distribution of lands to the poor, he arranged to send some of them to Carthage and some to Corinth. But he was assassinated shortly afterward by his enemies in the Roman Senate, and his son Augustus, finding this memorandum, built the present Carthage, not on the site of the old one, but very near it, in order to avoid the ancient curse. I have ascertained that he sent some 3000 colonists from Rome and that the rest came from the neighboring country. And thus the Romans took Africa away from the Carthaginians, destroyed Carthage, and re-peopled it again 102 years after its destruction.
Appian, [Punic Wars, 8.20.136](http://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text.jsp?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.01.0230%3Atext%3DPun.%3Achapter%3D20%3Asection%3D136)

A Carthaginian colony was delayed by Julius Caesar's assassination, until ~29 BCE when Augustus revived it. This coin from AD 10 from the Colonia Julia Carthago.

![Image 7: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_6e16abba8f394d31869984a7083d96a3~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_77,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_6e16abba8f394d31869984a7083d96a3~mv2.jpg)

**Roman Provincial Coins, Africa Proconsularis, Carthage**,  Augustus (27 BC-AD 14). Ae. D V Sp and P I Sp, Duovirs. Struck ~AD 10.

**Obv:** IMP(erator) C(aesar) D(ivi) f(ilius) A(ugustus) P(ontifex) M(aximus) P(ater) P(atriae), Bear Head Left

Translation: Emperor Caesar, Son of the Divine, Augustus, Chief Priest, Father of the Fatherland

**Rev:** P(ublius) I(—) SP(—) D(ecimus) V(—) SP(—) II VIR(i) C(olonia) I(ulia) C(arthago) P(ecunia) P(ublica) D(ecreto) D(ecurionum)

Translation: Publius I— SP— (and) Decimus V— SP—, Duovirs, the Julian Colony of Carthage, Public Money, by Decree of the Decurions

and this Roman coin 3 centuries later with a personified Carthage on the reverse, issued from Roman Carthage.

![Image 8: ree](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/62a3d9_b3f5e8754b7d4a85b3155cebc761c881~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_147,h_76,al_c,q_80,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,blur_2,enc_avif,quality_auto/62a3d9_b3f5e8754b7d4a85b3155cebc761c881~mv2.jpg)

Result
  • Roman victory
Territorial
changes		Roman conquest of all Carthaginian territories (except Numidia)
| | Belligerents | | [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") | [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") | The **Punic Wars** were a series of wars fought between the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") and the [Carthaginian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") during the period 264 to 146 BC. Three such wars took place, involving a total of forty-three years of warfare on both land and sea across the [western Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Western_Mediterranean&action=edit&redlink=1 "Western Mediterranean (page does not exist)") region, and a four-year-long [revolt against Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary_War "Mercenary War"). The [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") broke out on the Mediterranean island of [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") in 264 BC as a result of Rome's expansionary attitude combined with Carthage's proprietary approach to the island. At the start of the war Carthage was the dominant power of the western Mediterranean, with an extensive maritime empire (a [thalassocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalassocracy "Thalassocracy")), while Rome was a rapidly expanding power in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Italy "Roman Italy"), with a strong [army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_army_of_the_mid-Republic "Roman army of the mid-Republic") but no navy. The fighting took place primarily on Sicily and its surrounding waters, as well as in [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa"), [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") and [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia"). It lasted twenty-three years, until 241 BC, when the Carthaginians were defeated. By the terms of the [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lutatius "Treaty of Lutatius") Carthage paid large [reparations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_reparations "War reparations") and Sicily was annexed as the [first Roman province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilia_/(Roman_province/) "Sicilia (Roman province)"). The end of the war sparked a major but eventually unsuccessful revolt within Carthaginian territory known as the [Mercenary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary_War "Mercenary War"). The [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") began in 218 BC and witnessed the Carthaginian general [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal")'s [crossing of the Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") and invasion of mainland Italy. This expedition enjoyed considerable early success and campaigned in Italy for fourteen years before the survivors withdrew. There was also extensive fighting in [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians") (modern Spain and Portugal), Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa. The successful [Roman invasion of the Carthaginian homeland in Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_/(204%E2%80%93201_BC/) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") in 204 BC led to Hannibal's recall. He was defeated in the [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") in 202 BC and Carthage [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace"). A treaty was agreed in 201 BC which stripped Carthage of its overseas territories and some of its African ones, imposed a large indemnity, severely restricted the size of [its armed forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_Carthage "Military of Carthage") and prohibited Carthage from waging war without Rome's express permission. This caused Carthage to cease to be a military threat to Rome. In 151 BC Carthage attempted to defend itself against [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidia "Numidia") encroachments; Rome used this as a justification to declare war in 149 BC, starting the [Third Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War "Third Punic War"). This conflict was fought entirely on Carthaginian territory in what is now Tunisia and centred on the [siege of Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Carthage_/(Third_Punic_War/) "Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War)"). In 146 BC the Romans stormed the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage"), [sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting") it, slaughtered or enslaved its population and completely demolished the city. The Carthaginian territories were taken over as the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_/(Roman_province/) "Africa (Roman province)"). The ruins of the city lie east of modern [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") on the North African coast. Primary sources --------------- [![Image 2: A monochrome relief stele depicting a man in classical Greek clothing raising one arm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Stele_des_Polybios.jpg/250px-Stele_des_Polybios.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stele_des_Polybios.jpg) Polybius[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelfi2017192-1) The most reliable source for the Punic Wars[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-3) is the historian [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") (c. 200 – c. 118 BC), a Greek sent to Rome in 167 BC as a hostage.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4) He is best known for [_The Histories_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Histories_/(Polybius/) "The Histories (Polybius)"), written sometime after 146 BC.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalbank199011%E2%80%9312-5) Polybius was an [analytical historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historian#History_analysis "Historian") and wherever possible interviewed participants from both sides in the events he wrote about.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShutt193855-6)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201598,_101-7) He accompanied his [patron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage_in_ancient_Rome "Patronage in ancient Rome") and friend,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstin20065-8) the Roman general [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), in North Africa during the Third Punic War;[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201596,_108-9) modern historians consider Polybius to have treated Scipio and his relatives unduly favourably, but the consensus is to accept his account largely at face value.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi,_82%E2%80%9384-10) [Craige Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craige_B._Champion "Craige B. Champion") describes him as "a remarkably well-informed, industrious and insightful historian",[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion2015102-11) while the classicist [Adrian Goldsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Goldsworthy "Adrian Goldsworthy") states that "Polybius' account is usually to be preferred when it differs with any of our other accounts".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621-12) Polybius's work is considered broadly objective in spite of his pro-Roman point of view.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi-13)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles201116-14)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHau201623%E2%80%9324-15) The details of the wars in modern sources are largely based on interpretations of Polybius's account.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi,_82%E2%80%9384-10)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985432-16) The other major source commonly used by modern historians, particularly where Polybius's account is not extant, is the Roman historian [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy "Livy"). Livy relied heavily on Polybius, but wrote in a more structured way, with more details about Roman politics, as well as being openly pro-Roman.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-17)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200622-18)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201595-19)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoeHornblower20208%E2%80%9313-20) His accounts of military encounters are often demonstrably inaccurate; the classicist [Adrian Goldsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Goldsworthy "Adrian Goldsworthy") says Livy's "reliability is often suspect",[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222-21) and the historian [Philip Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sabin "Philip Sabin") refers to Livy's "military ignorance".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199662-22) Other, later ancient histories of the wars also exist, often in fragmentary or summary form.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621%E2%80%9323-23) Modern historians usually take into account the writings of various Roman [annalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annalists "Annalists"), some contemporary; the [Sicilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") Greek [Diodorus Siculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus"); and later writers such as[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201595-19) [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch"), [Appian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian "Appian"), and [Dio Cassius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassius_Dio "Cassius Dio").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015111%E2%80%93127-24)[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-25) No primary sources written from a Carthaginian point of view have survived,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20117-26) although elements of some – such as [Philinus of Agrigentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philinus_of_Agrigentum "Philinus of Agrigentum") – can be found in the works of some of the pro-Roman writers, especially Polybius.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201599-27) Other sources include coins, inscriptions, archaeological evidence and empirical evidence from reconstructions, such as the [trireme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trireme "Trireme") [_Olympias_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympias_/(trireme/) "Olympias (trireme)").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200623,_98-28) Background and origin --------------------- [![Image 3: a colour of the western Mediterranean region showing the areas under Roman and Carthaginian control in 264 BC](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/First_Punic_War_264_BC_v3.png/500px-First_Punic_War_264_BC_v3.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Punic_War_264_BC_v3.png) The map shows the approximate extent of territory controlled by Rome, Carthage and Syracuse immediately before the start of the First Punic War. Rome is shown in red, Carthage in grey, and Syracuse in green. The [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") had been [aggressively expanding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_expansion_in_Italy "Roman expansion in Italy") in the southern Italian mainland for a century before the [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011157%E2%80%93158-29) By 270 BC, when the last Greek cities of southern Italy ([Magna Graecia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Graecia "Magna Graecia")) submitted after the conclusion of the [Pyrrhic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrrhic_War "Pyrrhic War"), it had conquered all of peninsular Italy south of the [Arno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arno "Arno") River.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199921%E2%80%9322-30) During this period of Roman expansion Carthage, with its capital in what is now [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia"), had come to dominate southern [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians") (modern Spain and Portugal), much of the coastal regions of North Africa, the [Balearic Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_Islands "Balearic Islands"), [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica"), [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia") and the western half of Sicily in a maritime empire (a [thalassocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalassocracy "Thalassocracy")).[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200629%E2%80%9330-31) Beginning in 480 BC Carthage fought a [series of inconclusive wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_Wars "Sicilian Wars") against the Greek [city-states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state") of Sicily, led by [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_Sicily "Syracuse, Sicily").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011115,_132-32) By 264 BC Carthage was in control of much of the island, especially in the south and the west. Carthage and Rome were the preeminent powers in the western Mediterranean.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200625%E2%80%9327-33) Relations were good and the two states had several times declared their mutual friendship in [formal alliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaties_between_Rome_and_Carthage "Treaties between Rome and Carthage"): in 509 BC, 348 BC and around 279 BC. There were strong commercial links. During the Pyrrhic War of 280–275 BC, against a king of [Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epirus "Epirus") who alternately fought Rome in Italy and Carthage on Sicily, Carthage provided [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel") to the Romans and on at least one occasion provided its navy to ferry a Roman force.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles201194,_160,_163,_164%E2%80%93165-34)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200669%E2%80%9370-35) As Rome and Carthage came closer to sharing a joint border the chances of misunderstandings and hostilities increased. In the event they stumbled into war more by accident than design, with neither anticipating a prolonged conflict.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011175%E2%80%93176-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015c145%E2%80%93147-37)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200671%E2%80%9372-38) Opposing forces --------------- ### Armies [![Image 4: A monochrome relief stele depicting two figures dressed as Roman legionaries](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Altar_Domitius_Ahenobarbus_Louvre_n3_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Altar_Domitius_Ahenobarbus_Louvre_n3_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Altar_Domitius_Ahenobarbus_Louvre_n3_/(cropped/).jpg) Detail from the second century BC [Ahenobarbus relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_of_Domitius_Ahenobarbus "Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus") showing two Roman foot-soldiers Male Roman citizens who met a property requirement were liable for military service. Most were eligible and would serve as infantry, with a [better-off minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equites "Equites") providing a cavalry component.[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-40) Traditionally, when at war the Romans would raise two [legions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion "Roman legion"), each of 4,200 infantry[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-43) and 300 cavalry. Approximately 1,200 members of the infantry – poorer or younger men unable to afford the armour and equipment of a standard [legionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legionary "Legionary") – served as [javelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin "Javelin")\-armed [skirmishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skirmisher "Skirmisher") known as [velites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velites "Velites"); they each carried several javelins, which would be thrown from a distance, as well as a short sword and a large circular shield.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200648-44) The rest of the soldiers were equipped as [heavy infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_infantry "Heavy infantry"), with [body armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_armor "Body armor"), a large [shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutum_/(shield/) "Scutum (shield)") and [short thrusting swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladius "Gladius"). They were divided into three ranks: the [front rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastati "Hastati") also carried two javelins, while the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principes "Principes") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triari "Triari") ranks had a [thrusting spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasta_/(spear/) "Hasta (spear)") instead. Both legionary [sub-units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maniple_/(military_unit/) "Maniple (military unit)") and individual legionaries fought in relatively open order. It was the long-standing Roman procedure to elect two men each year as senior [magistrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_magistrate "Roman magistrate"), known as [consuls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul"), who in a time of war would each lead an army. An army was usually formed by combining a Roman legion with a similarly sized and equipped legion provided by their [Italian allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socii "Socii"); allied legions usually had a larger attached complement of cavalry than Roman ones.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922%E2%80%9325-45)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-46)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200141-47) Carthaginian citizens only served in their army if there was a direct threat to the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby19989-48)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006494-49) When they did they fought as well-armoured heavy infantry armed with long thrusting spears, although they were notoriously ill-trained and ill-disciplined. In most circumstances Carthage recruited foreigners to make up its army.[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-51) Many were from North Africa and these are usually referred to as Libyans. The region provided several types of fighters, including: [close-order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_order_formation "Close order formation") infantry equipped with large shields, helmets, short swords and long thrusting [spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear "Spear"); javelin-armed [light-infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-infantry "Light-infantry") skirmishers; close-order [shock cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_cavalry "Shock cavalry")[\[note 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-53) (also known as heavy cavalry) carrying spears; and [light cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_cavalry "Light cavalry"), skirmishers who threw javelins from a distance and avoided close combat; the latter were usually [Numidians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200631%E2%80%9334-54)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201579%E2%80%9387-55) The close-order African infantry and the citizen-militia both fought in a tightly-packed formation known as a [phalanx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phalanx "Phalanx").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-56) On occasion some of the infantry would wear captured Roman armour, especially among the troops of the Carthaginian general [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal").[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015305-57) In addition both [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians") and [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul") provided many experienced infantry and cavalry. The infantry from these areas were unarmoured troops who would charge ferociously, but had a reputation for breaking off if a combat was protracted.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-58)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19999-59) The Gallic cavalry, and possibly some of the Iberians, wore armour and fought as close-order troops; most or all of the mounted Iberians were light cavalry.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200713-60) [Slingers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_slinger "Balearic slinger") were frequently recruited from the Balearic Islands.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632-61)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19998-62) The Carthaginians also employed [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant"); North Africa had indigenous [African forest elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_forest_elephant "African forest elephant") at the time.[\[note 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-64)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19999-59)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199627-65) Garrison duty, [foraging](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Forage_\(militaty\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Forage (militaty) (page does not exist)") and land [blockades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade "Blockade") were the most common operations.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682,_311,_313%E2%80%93314-66)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999237-67) When armies were campaigning, surprise attacks, [ambushes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush "Ambush") and [stratagems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruse_de_guerre "Ruse de guerre") were common.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-56)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200655-68) Armies of the time consumed large amounts of resources, in particular food.[\[note 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-70) This could be supplied from stockpiles, either continuously taken to an army by pack animals or by army marching to its supply base at frequent intervals. Stockpiling the necessary quantities posed its own problems given the limited means of transportation of the time. Moving such bulk cargos was easier and swifter by sea, and was much preferred. The alternative, especially favoured in enemy territory, was to gather in what resources were locally available, which is known as foraging. If enemy forces were near this needed to be carried out in a controlled way, to prevent presenting easy opportunities for them to attack. Cavalry superiority made it much easier to protect ones own foragers or harass the enemy's. A large force relying on foraging would need to move frequently as they stripped the local countryside bare.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201569%E2%80%9370-71) [Formal battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle") were usually preceded by the two armies camping two–twelve kilometres (1–7 miles) apart for days or weeks; sometimes both forming up in battle order each day. If either commander felt at a disadvantage, he might march off without engaging; in such circumstances it was difficult to force a battle.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200656-72)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199664-73) Forming up in battle order was a complicated and premeditated affair, which took several hours. Infantry were usually positioned in the centre of the battle line, with light-infantry skirmishers to their front and cavalry on each flank.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200657-74) Many battles were decided when one side's infantry force was [attacked in the flank or rear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanking_maneuver "Flanking maneuver") and it was partially or wholly [enveloped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelopment "Envelopment").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-56)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199666-75) ### Navies [![Image 5: A diagram showing the location and usage of a corvus on a Roman galley.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Corvus.svg/250px-Corvus.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Corvus.svg) [Quinqueremes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinqueremes "Quinqueremes") were large and powerful-for-their-time warships[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200698-76) which provided the main components of the Roman and Carthaginian fleets throughout the Punic Wars.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199627%E2%80%9328-77) So ubiquitous was the type that Polybius uses it as a shorthand for "warship" in general.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006104-78) A quinquereme carried a crew of 300: 280 oarsmen and 20 deck crew and officers.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006100-79) It would also normally carry a complement of 40 marines;[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985435-80) if battle was thought to be imminent this would be increased to as many as 120.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson1995121-81)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006102%E2%80%93103-82) In 260 BC the Romans set out to construct a [fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_navy "Roman navy") and used a shipwrecked Carthaginian quinquereme as a blueprint for their own.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200697,_99%E2%80%93100-83)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985436_n._6-84) The Romans and their allies were unaccustomed to building quinqueremes and their early efforts were heavier than the Carthaginian vessels; thus they were slower and less manoeuvrable.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurray201169-85) Getting the oarsmen to row as a unit, let alone to execute more complex battle manoeuvres, required long and arduous training.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson1995278%E2%80%93280-86)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_Souza2008359-87) As a result, the Romans were initially at a disadvantage against the more experienced Carthaginians. To counter this, the Romans introduced the [corvus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corvus_/(weapon/) "Corvus (weapon)"), a bridge 1.2 metres (4 feet) wide and 11 metres (36 feet) long, with a heavy spike on the underside, designed to pierce and anchor into an enemy ship's deck.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson1995121-81) This allowed Roman legionaries acting as marines to [board enemy ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_boarding "Naval boarding") and capture them, rather than employing the previously [more common tactic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_tactics_in_the_Age_of_Galleys "Naval tactics in the Age of Galleys") of [ramming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramming "Ramming").[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011178-88) All warships were equipped with rams, a triple set of 60-centimetre-wide (2 ft) bronze blades weighing up to 270 kilograms (600 lb) positioned at the waterline. In the century prior to the Punic Wars, boarding had become increasingly common and ramming had declined, as the [larger and heavier vessels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic-era_warships "Hellenistic-era warships") adopted in this period increasingly lacked the speed and manoeuvrability necessary to ram effectively, while their sturdier construction reduced a ram's effect on them even in case of a successful attack. The Roman adaptation of the corvus was a continuation of this trend and compensated for their initial disadvantage in ship-manoeuvring skills. The added weight in the prow compromised both the ship's manoeuvrability and its seaworthiness, and in rough sea conditions the corvus became useless; part way through the First Punic War the Romans ceased using it.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011178-88)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWallinga195677%E2%80%9390-89)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006100%E2%80%93101,_103-90) First Punic War, 264–241 BC --------------------------- ### Course Much of the First Punic War was fought on or in the waters near Sicily.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006310-91) Away from the coasts its hilly and rugged terrain made manoeuvring large forces difficult, which encouraged defensive strategies. Land operations were largely confined to [raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raid_/(military/) "Raid (military)"), [sieges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege") and [interdiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interdiction "Interdiction"); in twenty-three years of war on Sicily there were only two full-scale pitched battles.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-92) #### Sicily, 264–257 BC [![Image 6: A relief map of Sicily showing the main cities at the time of the First Punic War](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Sicilia_-_prima_guerra_punica_key_en.svg/500px-Sicilia_-_prima_guerra_punica_key_en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sicilia_-_prima_guerra_punica_key_en.svg) Sicily, the main theatre of the First Punic War The spark that ignited the First Punic War in 264 BC was the issue of control of the independent Sicilian city-state of Messana (modern Messina),[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200674%E2%80%9375-93)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarmington1993168-94) with the Romans gaining control of the city and a foothold on Sicily at the [battle of Messana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Messana "Battle of Messana").[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199952%E2%80%9353-95) They then pressed Syracuse, the only substantial independent power on the island, into allying with them[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmeling201556-96)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015368-97) and laid siege to Carthage's main base, Agrigentum (modern [Agrigento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agrigento "Agrigento")) on the south coast.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011179-98) A Carthaginian army of 50,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 60 elephants attempted to lift the siege in 262 BC, but was badly defeated at the [battle of Agrigentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agrigentum "Battle of Agrigentum"). The Carthaginian garrison escaped during the night after the battle and the Romans seized the city and its inhabitants, selling 25,000 of them [into slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_ancient_Rome "Slavery in ancient Rome").[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011179%E2%80%93180-99) After this the land war on Sicily reached a stalemate as the Carthaginians focused on defending their well-fortified towns and cities; these were mostly on the coast and so could be supplied and reinforced without the Romans being able to use their superior army to interfere.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199964%E2%80%9366-100)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200697-101) The focus of the war shifted to the sea, where the Romans had less experience. On the few occasions they had previously felt the need for a naval presence greater than anti-piracy squadrons they had relied on their Latin or Greek allies for larger warships.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011179-98)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199966-102)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200691%E2%80%9392,_97-103) But the Romans did have extensive commercial maritime experience and access to a large pool of experienced sailors and [shipwrights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipwright "Shipwright") enabling them to rapidly build a navy to challenge Carthage's,[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201724%E2%80%9326-104)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPotter201464%E2%80%9365-105)[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011180%E2%80%93181-106) Using this navy and the corvus the Romans won a major victory at the [battle of Mylae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mylae "Battle of Mylae") in 260 BC.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006109%E2%80%93110-107)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199965-108)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199673%E2%80%9374-109) A Carthaginian base on Corsica was seized, but an attack on Sardinia was repulsed; the base on Corsica was then lost.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199963%E2%80%9365-110) In 258 BC a Roman fleet defeated a smaller Carthaginian fleet at the [battle of Sulci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sulci "Battle of Sulci") off the western coast of Sardinia.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199965-108) #### Africa, 256–255 BC Taking advantage of their naval victories the Romans launched an invasion of North Africa in 256 BC,[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015155-111) which the Carthaginians intercepted at the [battle of Cape Ecnomus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Ecnomus "Battle of Cape Ecnomus") off the southern coast of Sicily. The Carthaginians' superior seamanship was not as effective as they had hoped, while the Romans' corvuses gave them an edge as the battle degenerated into a shapeless brawl.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006102%E2%80%93103-82)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985435,_459-112) The Carthaginians were again beaten[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015155%E2%80%93156-113) in what was possibly the [largest naval battle in history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_naval_battle_in_history "Largest naval battle in history") by the number of combatants involved.[\[note 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-117)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006110%E2%80%93111-114)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199687-115)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985436-116) The invasion initially went well and in 255 BC the Carthaginians [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace"); the proposed terms were so harsh they decided to fight on.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200687-118) At the [battle of Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bagradas_River_/(255_BC/) "Battle of the Bagradas River (255 BC)") in spring 255 BC a combined force of infantry, cavalry and war elephants under the command of the [Spartan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta "Sparta") mercenary [Xanthippus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanthippus_of_Carthage "Xanthippus of Carthage") crushed the Romans.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011188-119) The Romans sent a fleet to evacuate their survivors and the Carthaginians opposed it at the [battle of Cape Hermaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Hermaeum "Battle of Cape Hermaeum") (modern [Cape Bon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bon "Cape Bon")); the Carthaginians were again heavily defeated.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps2003382-120) The Roman fleet, in turn, [was devastated by a storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_Roman_fleet_/(255_BC/) "Sinking of the Roman fleet (255 BC)") while returning to Italy, losing most of its ships and more than 100,000 men.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985438-121)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011189-122)[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201566-123) It is possible that the presence of the corvus, making the Roman ships unusually [unseaworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unseaworthy "Unseaworthy"), contributed to this disaster; there is no record of their being used again.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006557-124)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996112,_117-125) #### Sicily, 255–241 BC [![Image 7: A small, white statuette of an elephant with a mahout](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Pompeii%2C_Statuette_of_a_war_elephant.jpg/250px-Pompeii%2C_Statuette_of_a_war_elephant.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pompeii,_Statuette_of_a_war_elephant.jpg) The war continued, with neither side able to gain a decisive advantage.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006559-127) The Carthaginians attacked and recaptured Akragas in 255 BC, but not believing they could hold the city they razed and abandoned it.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996114%E2%80%93116,_169-128)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015158-129) The Romans rapidly rebuilt their fleet, adding 220 new ships, and captured Panormus (modern [Palermo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palermo "Palermo")) in 254 BC.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199980-130) The next year they lost another 150 ships to a storm.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011189%E2%80%93190-131) On Sicily the Romans avoided battle in 252 and 251 BC, according to Polybius because they feared the war elephants which the Carthaginians had shipped to the island.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996118-132)[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015159-133) In 250 BC the Carthaginians advanced on Panormus, but in a [battle outside the walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Panormus "Battle of Panormus") the Romans drove off the Carthaginian elephants with javelins. The elephants routed through the Carthaginian infantry, who were then charged by the Roman infantry to complete their defeat.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015159-133)[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996169-134) Slowly the Romans had occupied most of Sicily; in 250 BC they besieged the last two Carthaginian strongholds – [Lilybaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilybaeum "Lilybaeum") and [Drepana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drepana "Drepana") in the extreme west.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011190-135) Repeated attempts to storm Lilybaeum's strong walls failed, as did attempts to block access to its harbour, and the Romans [settled down to a siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lilybaeum_/(250%E2%80%93241_BC/) "Siege of Lilybaeum (250–241 BC)") which was to last nine years.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996127-136)[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199984%E2%80%9386-137) They launched a surprise attack on the Carthaginian fleet, but were defeated at the [battle of Drepana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Drepana "Battle of Drepana"); Carthage's greatest naval victory of the war.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006117%E2%80%93121-138) Carthage turned to the maritime offensive, inflicting another heavy naval defeat at the [battle of Phintias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Phintias "Battle of Phintias") and all but swept the Romans from the sea.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199988%E2%80%9391-139) It was to be seven years before Rome again attempted to field a substantial fleet, while Carthage put most of its ships into [reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_fleet "Reserve fleet") to save money and free up manpower.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006121%E2%80%93122-140)[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015163-141) #### Roman victory, 243–241 BC After more than 20 years of war, both states were financially and demographically exhausted.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBringmann2007127-142) Evidence of Carthage's financial situation includes their request for a 2,000-talent loan[\[note 10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-145) from [Ptolemaic Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemaic_Egypt "Ptolemaic Egypt"), which was refused.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199992-146)[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011193-147) Rome was also close to [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_default "Sovereign default") and the number of adult male citizens, who provided the manpower for the navy and the legions, had declined by 17 per cent since the start of the war.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199991-148) Goldsworthy describes Roman manpower losses as "appalling".[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006131-149) The Romans rebuilt their fleet again in 243 BC after the Senate approached Rome's wealthiest citizens for loans to finance the construction of one ship each, repayable from the [reparations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_reparations "War reparations") to be imposed on Carthage once the war was won.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199649-150) This new fleet effectively blockaded the Carthaginian garrisons.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006565-144) Carthage assembled a fleet which attempted to relieve them, but it was destroyed at the [battle of the Aegates Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Aegates_Islands "Battle of the Aegates Islands") in 241 BC,[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011196-151)[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199996-152) forcing the cut-off Carthaginian troops on Sicily to negotiate for peace.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006565-144)[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996157-153) The [Treaty of Lutatius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lutatius "Treaty of Lutatius") was agreed by which Carthage paid 3,200 talents of silver[\[note 11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-154) in reparations and [Sicily was annexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilia_/(Roman_province/) "Sicilia (Roman province)") as the first [Roman province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_province "Roman province").[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011196-151) Polybius regarded the war as "the longest, most continuous and most severely contested war known to us in history".[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002178-155) Henceforth Rome considered itself the leading military power in the western Mediterranean and increasingly the Mediterranean region as a whole.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006128%E2%80%93129,_357,_359%E2%80%93360-156) Interbellum, 241–218 BC ----------------------- ### Mercenary War [![Image 8: A map of the western Mediterranean showing the territory ceded to Rome by Carthage under the treaty.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/First_Punic_War_237_BC.jpg/500px-First_Punic_War_237_BC.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Punic_War_237_BC.jpg) Territory ceded to Rome by Carthage under the treaty is shown in pink The [Mercenary, or Truceless, War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary_War "Mercenary War") began in 241 BC as a dispute over the payment of wages owed to 20,000 foreign soldiers who had fought for Carthage on Sicily during the First Punic War. This erupted into full-scale mutiny under the leadership of [Spendius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spendius "Spendius") and [Matho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathos "Mathos"); 70,000 Africans from Carthage's oppressed dependent territories and towns flocked to join the mutineers, bringing supplies and finance.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999112%E2%80%93114-157)[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006133%E2%80%93134-158) Rome initially declined to take advantage of Carthage's troubles. Italians were prohibited from trading with the rebels[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006135%E2%80%93136-159)[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996173-160) and [Hiero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiero_II_of_Syracuse "Hiero II of Syracuse"), the king of the Roman satellite kingdom of [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_Sicily "Syracuse, Sicily"), was allowed to supply Carthage with the large amounts of food it needed and was no longer able to obtain from its hinterland.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996173-160)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006568-161) War-weary Carthage fared poorly in the initial engagements, especially under the generalship of [Hanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanno_II_the_Great "Hanno II the Great").[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein20176-162)[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999115-163) [Hamilcar Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilcar_Barca "Hamilcar Barca"), a veteran of the campaigns in Sicily, was given joint command of the army in 240 BC and supreme command in 239 BC.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999115-163) He campaigned successfully, initially demonstrating leniency in an attempt to woo the rebels over.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999118-164) To prevent this, in 240 BC Spendius tortured 700 Carthaginian prisoners to death and henceforth the war was pursued with great brutality.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011208-165)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein20177-166) By early 237 BC, after numerous setbacks, the rebels were defeated and their towns brought back under Carthaginian rule.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2000377-167) An expedition was prepared to reoccupy Sardinia, where mutinous soldiers had slaughtered all Carthaginians. The Roman Senate stated they considered the preparation of this force an act of war and demanded Carthage cede Sardinia and Corsica and pay an additional 1,200-talent indemnity.[\[note 12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-168)[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006569-169)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011209,_212%E2%80%93213-170) Weakened by 30 years of war, Carthage agreed rather than again enter into conflict with Rome.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996175-171) Polybius considered this "contrary to all justice" and modern historians have variously described the Romans' behaviour as "unprovoked aggression and treaty-breaking",[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006569-169) "shamelessly opportunistic"[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006136-172) and an "unscrupulous act".[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999124-173) These events fuelled resentment of Rome in Carthage, which was not reconciled to Rome's perception of its situation. This breach of the recently signed treaty was to be one the greatest causes of war with Carthage breaking out again in 218 BC in the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War").[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-174)[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015211-175)[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011213-176) ### Carthaginian expansion in Iberia [![Image 9: Image of both sides of a coin: one depicting a man's head; the other an elephant](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Carthage%2C_quarter_shekel%2C_237-209_BC%2C_SNG_BM_Spain_102.jpg/250px-Carthage%2C_quarter_shekel%2C_237-209_BC%2C_SNG_BM_Spain_102.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carthage,_quarter_shekel,_237-209_BC,_SNG_BM_Spain_102.jpg) With the suppression of the rebellion, Hamilcar understood that Carthage needed to strengthen its economic and military base if it were to again confront Rome.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos201577-178) After the First Punic War, Carthaginian possessions in Iberia were limited to a handful of prosperous coastal cities in the south.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos201580-179) Hamilcar took the army which he had led in the Mercenary War to Iberia in 237 BC and carved out a [quasi-monarchicial, autonomous state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_Iberia "Carthaginian Iberia") in its south east.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011220-180) This gave Carthage the silver mines, agricultural wealth, [manpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manpower "Manpower"), military facilities such as [shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipyard "Shipyard") and territorial depth to stand up to future Roman demands with confidence.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011219%E2%80%93220,_225-181)[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein2006173%E2%80%93174-182) Hamilcar ruled as a [viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy "Viceroy") and was succeeded by his son-in-law, [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Fair "Hasdrubal the Fair"), in the early 220s BC and then his son, [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"), in 221 BC.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011222,_225-183) In 226 BC the [Ebro Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_Treaty "Ebro Treaty") was agreed with Rome, specifying the [Ebro River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_River "Ebro River") as the northern boundary of the Carthaginian [sphere of influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_of_influence "Sphere of influence").[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006143%E2%80%93144-184) At some time during the next six years Rome made a separate agreement with the city of [Saguntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saguntum "Saguntum"), which was situated well south of the Ebro.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144-185) Second Punic War, 218–201 BC ---------------------------- In 219 BC a Carthaginian army under Hannibal [besieged, captured and sacked Saguntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Saguntum "Siege of Saguntum")[\[note 13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-186)[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-174)[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144%E2%80%93145-187) and in spring 218 BC Rome [declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_war "Declaration of war") on Carthage.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006145-188) There is scholarly debate as to whether Hannibal deliberately provoked the Romans with this attack or if the Romans were not concerned with any perceived impact on their amour propre as much as using the episode as a pretext to militarily curb Carthaginian expansion.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011234-189) There were three main [military theatres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theater_/(military/) "Theater (military)") in the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War"): Italy, where Hannibal defeated the Roman legions repeatedly, with occasional subsidiary campaigns in Sicily, Sardinia and Greece; Iberia, where [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_/(Barcid/) "Hasdrubal (Barcid)"), a younger brother of Hannibal, defended the Carthaginian colonial cities with mixed success before moving into Italy; and Africa, where the war was decided.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006310%E2%80%93311-190) ### Italy #### Hannibal crosses the Alps, 218–217 BC [![Image 10: a map of the western Mediterranean region showing the territory and allies of Rome and Carthage in 218 BC](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg/500px-Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg) The territory and allies of Rome and Carthage immediately before the start of the Second Punic War. In 218 BC there was some naval skirmishing in the waters around Sicily; the Romans [defeated a Carthaginian attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lilybaeum "Battle of Lilybaeum")[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200661-191)[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015327-192) and [captured the island of Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Malta_/(218_BC/) "Capture of Malta (218 BC)").[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastillo200625-193) In [Cisalpine Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisalpine_Gaul "Cisalpine Gaul") (modern northern Italy), the major [Gallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauls "Gauls") tribes attacked the Roman colonies there, causing the Roman settlers to flee to their previously established colony of Mutina (modern [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena")), where they were besieged. A Roman relief force broke through the siege, but was then ambushed and itself besieged.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006151-194) A Roman army had been assembled to campaign in Iberia; one Roman and one allied legion was detached from it and sent to northern Italy. Raising fresh troops to replace these delayed the army's departure for Iberia until September.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006151%E2%80%93152-195) Meanwhile, Hannibal assembled a Carthaginian army in New Carthage (modern [Cartagena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Spain "Cartagena, Spain")) in Iberia and led it northwards along the coast in May or June. It entered Gaul and took an inland route, to avoid the Roman allies to the south.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200647-196) At the [battle of the Rhône crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Rh%C3%B4ne_Crossing "Battle of the Rhône Crossing") Hannibal defeated a force of local Gauls which sought to bar his way.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999161%E2%80%93162-197) A Roman fleet carrying the Iberian-bound army landed at Rome's ally Massalia (modern [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille "Marseille")) at the mouth of the Rhône,[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011252-198) but Hannibal evaded the Romans and they continued to Iberia.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199)[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015321-200) The Carthaginians reached the foot of the Alps by late autumn and [crossed them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") in 24 days, surmounting the difficulties of climate, terrain[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201572-201) and the [guerrilla tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_warfare "Guerrilla warfare") of the native tribes. The Carthaginians arrived in what is now [Piedmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piedmont "Piedmont"), northern Italy, in early November. They comprised 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and an unknown number of elephants – the survivors of the 37 with which they left Iberia. The Romans were still in their winter quarters. The Carthaginians' surprise entry into the Italian peninsula led to the cancellation of Rome's planned campaign for the following year: an invasion of Africa.[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011283%E2%80%93284-202)[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201571-203)[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b107-204) #### Roman defeats, 217–216 BC [![Image 11: a photograph of a marble head depicting Hannibal](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_%28cropped2%29.png/250px-Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_%28cropped2%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_/(cropped2/).png) Hannibal, as envisaged in 1704 The Carthaginians captured the chief settlement of the hostile [Taurini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taurini "Taurini") Gauls (in the area of modern [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin")) and seized its food stocks.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999171-205)[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006168-206) In late November the Carthaginian cavalry routed a Roman force of cavalry and light infantry at the [battle of Ticinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ticinus "Battle of Ticinus").[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011243-207) As a result, most of the Gallic tribes declared for the Carthaginian cause and Hannibal's army grew to 37,000 men.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006177%E2%80%93178-208) A large Roman army was lured into combat by Hannibal at the [battle of the Trebia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trebia "Battle of the Trebia"), encircled and
