destroyed.[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011243%E2%80%93244-209)[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999175%E2%80%93176-210) Some 10,000 Romans out of 42,000 were able to fight their way to safety; most of their comrades were killed or captured. Gauls now joined Hannibal's army in large numbers.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999175%E2%80%93176,_193-211)[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011270-212) The Romans stationed an army at [Arretium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arretium "Arretium") and one on the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic "Adriatic") coast to block Hannibal's advance into central Italy.[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011285-213)[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006182-214) In early spring 217 BC the Carthaginians crossed the [Apennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apennine_Mountains "Apennine Mountains") unopposed, taking a difficult but unguarded route.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006184-215) Hannibal attempted to draw the westernmost of the two Roman armies into a pitched battle by devastating the area it had been sent to protect.[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011244-216) This provoked its commander into ordering a hasty pursuit without proper reconnaissance. Hannibal set an ambush and in the [battle of Lake Trasimene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Trasimene "Battle of Lake Trasimene") completely defeated this Roman army, killing 15,000 Romans, including their commander, and taking 15,000 [prisoners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war"). A cavalry force of 4,000 from the Roman army based at Arretium was also engaged and wiped out.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006189%E2%80%93190-217)[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011244-216) The prisoners were badly treated if they were Romans, but released if they were from one of Rome's allies. Hannibal wished to stir up disaffection in the states which made up many of Rome's allies in Italy.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011270-212) These allied states provided more than half of Rome's military manpower.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015311%E2%80%93312-218) The Carthaginians marched deeper into Italy, hoping that the ethnic Greek and [Italic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_peoples_of_Italy "Ancient peoples of Italy") states of southern Italy in particular could be persuaded to [defect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defection "Defection").[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199886-219) The Romans, panicked by these heavy defeats, appointed [Fabius Maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Fabius_Maximus_Verrucosus "Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus") as [dictator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_dictator "Roman dictator"), with sole charge of the war effort.[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999183-220) Fabius introduced the [Fabian strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_strategy "Fabian strategy") of avoiding open battle with his opponent, but constantly skirmishing with small detachments of the enemy. This was not popular with parts of the Roman army, public and Senate, since he avoided battle while Italy was being devastated by the enemy.[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011285-213)[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006195%E2%80%93196-221) Hannibal marched through the richest and most fertile parts of Italy, hoping the devastation would draw Fabius into battle, but Fabius refused.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999184%E2%80%93188-222) In the 216 BC elections [Terentius Varro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Terentius_Varro "Gaius Terentius Varro") and [Aemilius Paullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Aemilius_Paullus_/(consul_219_BC/) "Lucius Aemilius Paullus (consul 219 BC)") were elected as consuls; both were more aggressively minded than Fabius.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011286-223)[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006199%E2%80%93200-224) The Roman Senate authorised the raising of a force of 86,000 men, the largest in Roman history to that point.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999191,_194-225)[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006198%E2%80%93199-226) Paullus and Varro marched southward to confront Hannibal, who accepted battle on the open plain near [Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannae "Cannae") in south-east Italy. In the [battle of Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae "Battle of Cannae") the Roman legions forced their way through Hannibal's deliberately weak centre, but Libyan heavy infantry on the wings swung around their advance, menacing their flanks. Another Carthaginian commander named [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal,_commander_of_the_service_corps "Hasdrubal, commander of the service corps") – not the same man as Hasdrubal Barca, one of Hannibal's younger brothers[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200764-227) – led the Carthaginian cavalry on the left wing which routed the Roman cavalry opposite. It then swept around the rear of the Romans to attack the cavalry on the other wing, before charging into the legions from behind. As a result, the Roman infantry was surrounded with no means of escape.[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011245-228) At least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999192%E2%80%93194-229) The historian Richard Miles describes Cannae as "Rome's greatest military disaster".[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011279-230) Toni Ñaco del Hoyo considers the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae to be the three "great military calamities" suffered by the Romans in the first three years of the war.[\[218\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-231) Brian Carey writes that these three defeats brought Rome to the brink of collapse.[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey20072-232) Within a few weeks of Cannae a Roman army of 25,000 was ambushed by [Boii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boii "Boii") Gauls at the [battle of Silva Litana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Silva_Litana "Battle of Silva Litana") and annihilated.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoberts2017vi%E2%80%931x-233) Fabius was elected consul in 215 BC and re-elected in 214 BC.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006227-234)[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199894,_99-235) #### Roman allies defect, 216–207 BC Little survives of Polybius's account of Hannibal's army in Italy after Cannae and Livy is the best surviving source for this part of the war.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-17)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222-21)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199662-22) Several of the city-states in southern Italy allied with Hannibal or were captured when pro-Carthaginian factions betrayed their defences. These included the large city of [Capua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capua "Capua") and the major port city of Tarentum (modern [Taranto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranto "Taranto")). Two of the major [Samnite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samnium "Samnium") tribes also joined the Carthaginian cause. By 214 BC the bulk of southern Italy had turned against Rome, although there were many exceptions. The majority of Rome's allies in central Italy remained loyal. All except the smallest towns were too well fortified for Hannibal to take by assault and blockade could be a long-drawn-out affair, or, if the target was a port, impossible. Carthage's new allies felt little sense of community with Carthage, or even with each other. The new allies increased the number of places that Hannibal's army was expected to defend from Roman retribution, but provided relatively few fresh troops to assist him in doing so. Such Italian forces as were raised resisted operating away from their home cities and performed poorly when they did.[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222%E2%80%93226-236)[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015313-237) [![Image 12: a map of southern peninsular Italy showing the maximum extent of Carthaginian control](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/61/Second_Punic_war_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Punic_war_/(cropped/).png) Hannibal's allies in southern Italy c. 213 BC, shown in light blue When the port city of [Locri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locri "Locri") defected to Carthage in the summer of 215 BC it was immediately used to reinforce the Carthaginian forces in Italy with soldiers, supplies and war elephants.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199898-238) It was the only time during the war that Hannibal received reinforcements from Carthage.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201575-239) A second force, under Hannibal's youngest brother [Mago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca"), was meant to land in Italy in 215 BC but was diverted to Iberia after the Carthaginian defeat there at the [battle of Dertosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dertosa "Battle of Dertosa").[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199898-238)[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015370-240) Meanwhile, the Romans took drastic steps to raise new legions: enrolling slaves, criminals and those who did not meet the usual property qualification.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006226-241) By early 215 BC they were fielding at least 12 legions; two years later they had 18; and a year after that, 22. By 212 BC the full complement of the legions deployed would have been in excess of 100,000 men, plus, as always, a similar number of allied troops. The majority were deployed in southern Italy in field armies of approximately 20,000 men each. This was insufficient to challenge Hannibal's army in open battle, but sufficient to force him to concentrate his forces and to hamper his movements.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006227-234) The war surged around southern Italy as cities went over to the Carthaginians or were taken by subterfuge and the Romans recaptured them by siege or by the support of pro-Roman factions.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222%E2%80%93235-242) Hannibal repeatedly defeated Roman armies; in 208 BC both consuls were killed in a cavalry skirmish. But wherever his main army was not active the Romans threatened Carthaginian-supporting towns or sought battle with Carthaginian or Carthaginian-allied detachments; frequently with success.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996158-143)[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006236-243) By 207 BC Hannibal had been confined to the extreme south of Italy and many of the cities and territories which had joined the Carthaginian cause had returned to their Roman allegiance.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006237%E2%80%93238-244) #### Greece, Sardinia and Sicily During 216 BC the Macedonian king, [Philip V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Macedon "Philip V of Macedon"), [pledged his support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian%E2%80%93Carthaginian_Treaty "Macedonian–Carthaginian Treaty") to Hannibal,[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999199%E2%80%93200-245) initiating the [First Macedonian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Macedonian_War "First Macedonian War") against Rome in 215 BC. In 211 BC Rome contained this threat by allying with the [Aetolian League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aetolian_League "Aetolian League"), a coalition of Greek city-states which was hostile towards Macedonia, and persuading them to participate in the war. In 205 BC this war ended with a [negotiated peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Phoenice "Treaty of Phoenice").[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006253%E2%80%93260-246) A rebellion in support of the Carthaginians broke out on Sardinia in 213 BC, but it was quickly put down by the Romans.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011288-247) [![Image 13: a colourful mosaic of a sword-armed soldier gesturing to a seated man in ancient-style robes](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Archimedes_before_his_death_with_the_Roman_soldier%2C_Roman_mosaic.jpg/330px-Archimedes_before_his_death_with_the_Roman_soldier%2C_Roman_mosaic.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Archimedes_before_his_death_with_the_Roman_soldier,_Roman_mosaic.jpg) Archimedes before being killed by the Roman soldier – an early-modern mosaic Up to 215 BC Sicily remained firmly in Roman hands, preventing the easy seaborne reinforcement and resupply of Hannibal from Carthage. [Hiero II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiero_II_of_Syracuse "Hiero II of Syracuse"), the tyrant of Syracuse for the previous sixty years and a staunch Roman ally since 263 BC, died in 215 BC and his successor [Hieronymus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_of_Syracuse "Hieronymus of Syracuse") was discontented with his situation. Hannibal negotiated a treaty whereby Syracuse defected to Carthage, in exchange for a Carthaginian pledge to allow the whole of Sicily to become a Syracusan possession. The Syracusan army proved no match for a Roman army led by [Claudius Marcellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Claudius_Marcellus "Marcus Claudius Marcellus") and by spring 213 BC [Syracuse was besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Syracuse_/(213%E2%80%93212_BC/) "Siege of Syracuse (213–212 BC)").[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011327-248)[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999200-249) The siege was marked by the ingenuity of [Archimedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes "Archimedes") in inventing war machines to counteract the traditional siege warfare methods of the Romans.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011328-250) A large Carthaginian army led by [Himilco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himilco_/(fl._3rd_century_BC/) "Himilco (fl. 3rd century BC)") was sent to relieve the city in 213 BC.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011288-247)[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011329-251) It captured several Roman-garrisoned towns on Sicily; many Roman garrisons were either expelled or massacred by Carthaginian partisans. In spring 212 BC the Romans stormed Syracuse in a surprise night assault and captured several districts of the city. Meanwhile, the Carthaginian army was crippled by [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_/(disease/) "Plague (disease)"). After the Carthaginians failed to resupply the city, Syracuse fell that autumn; Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011329-251) Carthage sent more reinforcements to Sicily in 211 BC and went on the offensive. A fresh Roman army attacked the main Carthaginian stronghold on the island, [Agrigentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agrigentum "Agrigentum"), in 210 BC and the city was betrayed to the Romans by a discontented Carthaginian officer. The remaining Carthaginian-controlled towns then surrendered or were taken through force or treachery[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011330-252)[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006266%E2%80%93267-253) and the Sicilian grain supply to Rome and its armies was secured.[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015311-254) #### Italy, 207–203 BC In the spring of 207 BC [Hasdrubal Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Barca "Hasdrubal Barca") repeated the feat of his elder brother by marching an army of 35,000 men across the Alps and invading Italy. His aim was to join his forces with those of Hannibal, but Hannibal was unaware of his presence. The Romans facing Hannibal in southern Italy tricked him into believing the whole Roman army was still in camp, while a large portion marched north under the consul [Claudius Nero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Claudius_Nero "Gaius Claudius Nero") and reinforced the Romans facing Hasdrubal, who were commanded by the other consul, [Marcus Salinator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Livius_Salinator "Marcus Livius Salinator"). The combined Roman force attacked Hasdrubal at the [battle of the Metaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Metaurus "Battle of the Metaurus") and destroyed his army, killing Hasdrubal. This battle confirmed Roman dominance in Italy and marked the end of their Fabian strategy.[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011290-255)[\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011304%E2%80%93306-256) In 205 BC Mago landed in Genua (modern [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa")) in north-west Italy with the remnants of his Spanish army where it received Gallic and [Ligurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liguria "Liguria") reinforcements. Mago's arrival in the north of the Italian peninsula was followed by Hannibal's inconclusive [battle of Crotona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Crotona "Battle of Crotona") in 204 BC in the far south of the peninsula. Mago marched his reinforced army towards the lands of Carthage's main Gallic allies in the [Po Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po_Valley "Po Valley"), but was checked by a large Roman army and defeated at the [battle of Insubria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Insubria "Battle of Insubria") in 203 BC.[\[244\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999286%E2%80%93287-257) After a Roman army invaded the Carthaginian homeland in 204 BC, defeated the Carthaginians in two major battles and won the allegiance of the Numidian kingdoms of North Africa, Hannibal and the remnants of his army were recalled.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011310-258) They sailed from Croton (modern [Crotone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotone "Crotone"))[\[246\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006244-259) and landed at Carthage with 15,000–20,000 experienced veterans. Mago was also recalled; he died of wounds on the voyage and some of his ships were intercepted by the Romans,[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011312-260) but 12,000 of his troops reached Carthage.[\[248\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999289-261) ### Iberia #### Iberia, 218–209 BC The Roman fleet continued on from Massala in the autumn of 218 BC, landing the army it was transporting in north-east Iberia, where it won support among the local tribes.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199) A rushed Carthaginian attack in late 218 BC was beaten back at the [battle of Cissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cissa "Battle of Cissa").[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199)[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011321-262) In 217 BC 40 Carthaginian warships were defeated by 55 Roman and Massalian vessels at the [battle of the Ebro River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ebro_River "Battle of Ebro River"), with 29 Carthaginian ships lost. The Romans' [lodgement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodgement "Lodgement") between the Ebro and the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees") blocked the route from Iberia to Italy and greatly hindered the despatch of reinforcements from Iberia to Hannibal.[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011321-262) The Carthaginian commander in Iberia, Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal, marched into this area in 215 BC, offered battle and was [defeated at Dertosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ibera "Battle of Ibera"), although both sides suffered heavy casualties.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) The Carthaginians suffered a wave of defections of local [Celtiberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtiberians "Celtiberians") tribes to Rome.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199) The Roman commanders captured Saguntum in 212 BC and in 211 BC hired 20,000 Celtiberian mercenaries to reinforce their army. Observing that the three Carthaginian armies were deployed apart from each other, the Romans split their forces.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) This strategy resulted in two separate battles in 211 BC, usually referred to jointly as the [battle of the Upper Baetis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Upper_Baetis "Battle of the Upper Baetis"). Both battles ended in complete defeat for the Romans, as Hasdrubal had bribed the Romans' mercenaries to desert. The Romans pulled back to their coastal stronghold north of the Ebro, from which the Carthaginians again failed to expel them.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199)[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) Reinforcements arrived in 210 BC and stabilised the situation.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) [![Image 14: a black and white photograph of a marble bust of a man, with the nose broken off](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Bust_of_Sulla_%28loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek%29_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg/250px-Bust_of_Sulla_%28loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek%29_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bust_of_Sulla_/(loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek/)_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg) 2nd century BC marble bust, identified as Scipio Africanus[\[251\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoarelli200273%E2%80%9374-264)[\[252\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEtcheto2012274%E2%80%93278-265) In 210 BC [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") arrived in Iberia with further Roman reinforcements.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266) In a carefully planned assault in 209 BC [he captured New Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cartagena_/(209_BC/) "Battle of Cartagena (209 BC)"), the lightly-defended centre of Carthaginian power in Iberia.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266)[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011292-267) Scipio seized a vast booty of gold, silver and siege artillery, but released the captured population. He also liberated the Iberian hostages, who had been held there by the Carthaginians to ensure the loyalty of their tribes.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266)[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015362-268) Even so, many of them later fought against the Romans.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266) #### Roman victory in Iberia, 208–205 BC In the spring of 208 BC Hasdrubal moved to engage Scipio at the [battle of Baecula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baecula "Battle of Baecula").[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-269) The Carthaginians were defeated, but Hasdrubal was able to withdraw the majority of his army and prevent any Roman pursuit; most of his losses were among his Iberian allies. Scipio was not able to prevent Hasdrubal from leading his depleted army through the western passes of the Pyrenees into Gaul. In 207 BC, after recruiting heavily in Gaul, Hasdrubal crossed the Alps into Italy in an attempt to join his brother, Hannibal, but was defeated before he could.[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-269)[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200786%E2%80%9390-270)[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999211-271) In 206 BC at the [battle of Ilipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ilipa "Battle of Ilipa"), Scipio with 48,000 men, half Italian and half Iberian, defeated a Carthaginian army of 54,500 men and 32 elephants. This sealed the fate of the Carthaginians in Iberia.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266)[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011293-272) The last Carthaginian-held city in Iberia, Gades (modern [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz")), defected to the Romans.[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011303-273) Later the same year a [mutiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutiny_at_Sucro "Mutiny at Sucro") broke out among Roman troops, which attracted support from Iberian leaders, disappointed that Roman forces had remained in the peninsula after the expulsion of the Carthaginians, but it was effectively put down by Scipio. In 205 BC a last attempt was made by Mago to recapture New Carthage when the Roman occupiers were shaken by another mutiny and an Iberian uprising, but he was repulsed. Mago left Iberia for Cisalpine Gaul with his remaining forces.[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015362-268) In 203 BC Carthage succeeded in recruiting at least 4,000 mercenaries from Iberia, despite Rome's nominal control.[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011333-274) ### Africa In 213 BC [Syphax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syphax "Syphax"), a powerful [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") king in North Africa, declared for Rome. In response, Roman advisers were sent to train his soldiers and he waged war against the Carthaginian ally [Gala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gala_/(king/) "Gala (king)").[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) In 206 BC the Carthaginians ended this drain on their resources by dividing several Numidian kingdoms with him. One of those disinherited was the Numidian prince [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa"), who was thus driven into the arms of Rome.[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015372-275) #### Scipio's invasion of Africa, 204–201 BC [![Image 15: a terrain map of northern Tunisia, with the manoeuvres of Scipio's army in 204–203 BC superimposed on it](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png/500px-Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa,_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png) In 205 BC Publius Scipio was given command of the legions in Sicily and allowed to enrol volunteers for his plan to end the war by an invasion of Africa.[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286%E2%80%93288-276) Preparations were extensive: including thorough training of the soldiers involved and the stockpiling of a vast quantity of food. Scipio intended to largely feed his army from stockpiles in Sicily, [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia") and southern Italy, thus freeing it from the need to forage. War [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel") was also prepared in great quantities.[\[264\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287%E2%80%93288,_294-277) After [landing in Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_/(204%E2%80%93201_BC/) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") in 204 BC he was joined by Masinissa and a force of Numidian cavalry.[\[265\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291%E2%80%93292-278) The ships which had landed the Roman army returned to Sicily to pick up supplies; Scipio wished to build up a large stock of food and materiel in Africa.[\[266\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-279) In spring and summer 203 BC the Romans gave battle to two large Carthaginian armies and destroyed both.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011310-258) After the second of these, Syphax was pursued and taken prisoner by Masinissa at the [battle of Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"); Masinissa then seized most of Syphax's kingdom with Roman help.[\[267\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282%E2%80%93283-280) Rome and Carthage entered into peace negotiations and Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy.[\[268\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006298%E2%80%93300-281) The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy Carthage repudiated it.[\[269\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999287%E2%80%93291-282) Hannibal was placed in command of an army formed from his and Mago's veterans from Italy and newly raised troops from Africa, but with few cavalry.[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-283) The decisive [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") followed in October 202 BC.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-284)[\[272\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007119-285) Unlike most battles of the Second Punic War, the Romans had superiority in cavalry and the Carthaginians in infantry.[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-283) Hannibal attempted to use 80 elephants to break into the Roman infantry formation, but the Romans countered them effectively and they routed back through the Carthaginian ranks.[\[273\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999291%E2%80%93293-286) The Roman and allied Numidian cavalry then pressed their attacks and drove the Carthaginian cavalry from the field. The two sides' infantry fought inconclusively until the Roman cavalry returned and attacked the Carthaginian rear. The Carthaginian formation collapsed; Hannibal was one of the few to escape the field.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-284) The new peace treaty dictated by Rome stripped Carthage of all of its overseas territories and some of its African ones; an indemnity of 10,000 silver talents[\[note 14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-288) was to be paid over 50 years; hostages were to be taken; Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants and its fleet was restricted to 10 warships; it was prohibited from waging war outside Africa and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BC.[\[275\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006308%E2%80%93309-289) Henceforth it was clear that Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[\[276\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein2006176-290) Scipio was awarded a [triumph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") and received the _[agnomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus".[\[277\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011318-291) Under the pressure of the war, the Romans developed an increasingly effective system of logistics to equip and feed the unprecedented numbers of soldiers they fielded. During the last three years of the war this was extended to the transporting by sea from Sicily to Africa of almost all the requirements of Scipio's large army. These developments made possible the subsequent Roman overseas wars of conquest.[\[278\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006359%E2%80%93360-292) Interbellum, 201–149 BC ----------------------- At the end of the war, Masinissa emerged as by far the most powerful ruler among the Numidians.[\[279\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398-293) Over the following 48 years he repeatedly took advantage of Carthage's inability to protect its possessions. Whenever Carthage petitioned Rome for redress, or permission to take military action, Rome backed its ally, Masinissa, and refused.[\[280\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398,_407-294) Masinissa's seizures of and raids into Carthaginian territory became increasingly flagrant. In 151 BC Carthage raised an army, the treaty notwithstanding, and [counterattacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterattack "Counterattack") the Numidians. The campaign ended in disaster for the Carthaginians at the [battle of Oroscopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Oroscopa "Battle of Oroscopa") when their army surrendered.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-295) Carthage had paid off its indemnity and was prospering economically, but was no military threat to Rome.[\[282\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015408-296)[\[283\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015434-297) However, elements in the Roman Senate, led by [Cato the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_the_Elder "Cato the Elder"), had long wished to destroy Carthage and with the breach of the treaty as a _[casus belli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casus_belli "Casus belli")_, war was declared in 149 BC.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-295) Third Punic War, 149–146 BC --------------------------- In 149 BC a Roman army of approximately 50,000 men, jointly commanded by both consuls, landed near [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia"), 35 kilometres (22 mi) north of Carthage.[\[284\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015436%E2%80%93437-298) Rome demanded that if war were to be avoided, the Carthaginians must hand over all of their armaments. Vast amounts of materiel were delivered, including 200,000 sets of armour, 2,000 [catapults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballista#Early_Roman_ballistae "Ballista") and a large number of warships.[\[285\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015438-299) This done, the Romans demanded the Carthaginians burn their city and relocate at least 16 kilometres (10 mi) from the sea; the Carthaginians broke off negotiations and set to recreating their [armoury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal "Arsenal").[\[286\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999309%E2%80%93310-300) ### Siege of Carthage [![Image 16: a bronze head, believed by some experts to depict Scipio Aemilianus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Bronze_statue_of_a_Hellenistic_prince%2C_1st_half_of_2nd_century_BC%2C_found_on_the_Quirinal_in_Rome%2C_Palazzo_Massimo_alle_Terme%2C_Rome_%2831479801364%29.jpg/250px-Bronze_statue_of_a_Hellenistic_prince%2C_1st_half_of_2nd_century_BC%2C_found_on_the_Quirinal_in_Rome%2C_Palazzo_Massimo_alle_Terme%2C_Rome_%2831479801364%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_statue_of_a_Hellenistic_prince,_1st_half_of_2nd_century_BC,_found_on_the_Quirinal_in_Rome,_Palazzo_Massimo_alle_Terme,_Rome_/(31479801364/).jpg) As well as manning the walls of Carthage, the Carthaginians formed a [field army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_army "Field army") under [Hasdrubal the Boetharch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Boetharch "Hasdrubal the Boetharch"), which was based 25 kilometres (16 mi) to the south.[\[288\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015439-302)[\[289\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011343-303) The Roman army moved to lay siege to Carthage, but its walls were so strong and its citizen militia so determined it was unable to make any impact, while the Carthaginians struck back effectively. Their army raided the Roman [lines of communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_communication "Line of communication"),[\[289\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011343-303) and in 148 BC Carthaginian [fire ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_ship "Fire ship") destroyed many Roman vessels. The main Roman camp was in a swamp, which caused an outbreak of disease during the summer.[\[290\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999314-304) The Romans moved their camp, and their ships, further away – so they were now more blockading than closely besieging the city.[\[291\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999315-305) The war dragged on into 147 BC.[\[289\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011343-303) In early 147 BC [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), an adopted grandson of Scipio Africanus who had distinguished himself during the previous two years' fighting, was elected consul and took control of the war.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-295)[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-306) The Carthaginians continued to resist vigorously: they constructed warships and, during the summer, twice gave battle to the Roman fleet, losing both times.[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-306) The Romans launched an assault on the walls; after confused fighting they broke into the city, but, becoming disoriented in the dark, withdrew. Hasdrubal and his army retreated into the city to reinforce the garrison.[\[293\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006348%E2%80%93349-307) Hasdrubal had Roman prisoners tortured to death on the walls, in view of the Roman army. He was reinforcing the will to resist in the Carthaginian citizens; from this point there could be no possibility of negotiations. Some members of the city council denounced his actions and Hasdrubal had them put to death and took control of the city.[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-306)[\[294\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006349-308) With no Carthaginian army in the field, those cities which had remained loyal went over to the Romans or were captured.[\[295\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999318-309) Scipio moved back to a close blockade of the city and built a [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_/(architecture/) "Mole (architecture)") which cut off supply from the sea.[\[296\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20112-310) In the spring of 146 BC the Roman army managed to secure a foothold on the fortifications near the harbour.[\[297\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-311)[\[298\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011346-312) Scipio launched a major assault which quickly captured the city's main square, where the legions camped overnight.[\[299\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113-313) The next morning, the Romans started systematically working their way through the residential part of the city, killing everyone they encountered and burning the buildings behind them.[\[297\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-311) At times, the Romans progressed from rooftop to rooftop, to prevent missiles being hurled down on them.[\[299\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113-313) It took six days to clear the city of resistance; only on the last day did Scipio take prisoners. The last holdouts, including Roman [deserters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deserter "Deserter") in Carthaginian service, fought on from the Temple of [Eshmoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eshmun "Eshmun") and burnt it down around themselves when all hope was gone.[\[300\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113%E2%80%934-314) There were 50,000 Carthaginian prisoners, a small proportion of the pre-war population, who were sold into slavery.[\[301\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002316-315) There is a tradition that Roman forces then [sowed the city with salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salting_the_earth "Salting the earth"), but this has been shown to have been a 19th-century invention.[\[302\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERidley1986144%E2%80%93145-316)[\[303\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201450-317) Aftermath --------- [![Image 17: a colour photograph of a semi-urban area by the sea on a sunny day](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Carthage-1958-PortsPuniques.jpg/330px-Carthage-1958-PortsPuniques.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carthage-1958-PortsPuniques.jpg) The site of Carthage in 1958, showing the circular war harbour capable of holding 170 galleys.[\[296\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20112-310) Rome was determined that the city of Carthage remain in ruins. The Senate despatched a ten-man commission and Scipio was ordered to carry out further demolitions. A curse was placed on anyone who might attempt to resettle the site in the future.[\[304\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011353-318) The former site of the city was confiscated as _[ager publicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ager_publicus "Ager publicus")_, public land.[\[305\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443-319) The remaining Carthaginian territories were annexed by Rome and reconstituted to become the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Province "Africa Province") with Utica as its capital.[\[306\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002310,_316-320) The province became a major source of grain and other foodstuffs for Rome.[\[307\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhittaker1996596-321) Numerous large Punic cities, such as those in [Mauretania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauretania "Mauretania"), were taken over by the Romans,[\[308\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard2015249-322) although they were permitted to retain their Punic system of government and culture.[\[309\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFantar2015455%E2%80%93456-323) The Romans did not interfere in the locals' private lives and Punic culture, language and religion survived, and is known to modern scholars as "Neo-Punic civilization".[\[310\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443%E2%80%93445-324)[\[311\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFantar2015454-325) The [Punic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_language "Punic language") continued to be spoken in north Africa until the 7th century AD.[\[312\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJouhaud196822-326)[\[313\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard1955105-327) A century after the end of the Punic Wars, the site of Carthage was [rebuilt as a Roman city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Carthage "Roman Carthage") by [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar "Julius Caesar"); it became one of the main cities of Roman Africa by the time of the [Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire").[\[314\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERichardson2015480%E2%80%93481-328)[\[315\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011363%E2%80%93364-329) Rome still exists as the capital of Italy; the ruins of Carthage lie 24 kilometres (15 mi) east of [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") on the North African coast.[\[316\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006296-330)[\[317\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUNESCO2020-331) Notes, citations
